Recent research has strongly suggested that a pre-trained language model is transferable to other tasks such as a backbone network in a meta-learning framework. However, when this framework encounters new classes during testing, the classification task becomes complicated due to a lack of labeled samples, with some support classes potentially containing outlier samples that deviate from the others. To prevent the learning backbone from being misled by these outliers, we introduce an effective framework that achieves both FSL and outlier detection in support classes. To handle the outlier issue, we designed a support-class cleaning mechanism that utilizes the pre-trained knowledge to identify and filter out the outlier samples. Consequently, this framework contributes notable advancements for both FSL and outlier detection, with both tasks being implemented with a single model and without requiring any additional labeled data. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/bala3/FSL-Outlier-Detector.

We've found that localized electron and hole operators in a specific physical model have a connection to non-invertible charge defects in a different model that we've also studied. These operators act as a kind of "electromagnet" that alters the properties of these defects. As a result, we were able to understand the structure of these localized operators more deeply and verify a theoretical relation that was previously unknown. Additionally, this investigation has a broader implication: it suggests that the underlying physical properties of fundamental excitations remain the same regardless of the Hamiltonian's specific form, under a certain theoretical condition.

Orientability of certain graph types has been a topic of research for quite some time now. We focused on orienting split graphs, particularly those with semi-transitive properties, and devised a method to recognize when a split graph can be oriented without violating certain direction rules. We also investigated the complexity of finding such an orientation, if one exists, and found that this complexity varies depending on the input representation. Interestingly, orienting split graphs with a small independent set can be done in a reasonable time, but the process becomes much more challenging if the split graph has a large independent set. As an extension, we explored the similar problem of orienting chordal bipartite graphs, which are a more specific type of graph, and found that these graphs can be oriented in a reasonable time.

Our research aims to measure both the efficiency of identifying real versus fake tau leptons and the efficiency of identifying genuine versus misidentified jets. This study utilizes Intergenerational Studies of Vector Boson Production in Electroweak Boson Scattering events, analyzing a dataset of 31.2 fb^-1 at 13 TeV. To verify a leptonic decay pattern, we employ a novel approach that combines three distinct methods: One particle-in-hole, One loop below threshold, and One loop above threshold. These strategies allow for enhanced sensitivity, particularly in cases where quarks are misidentified as tau leptons. Latest results show that tau leptons are correctly identified with 96.7% efficiency, whereas misidentified jets are correctly identified with 49.3% efficiency. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that IncLBT exhibits the highest sensitivity at 1 sigma, followed by OLTB at 0.5 sigma, and OLAT at 0.3 sigma.

Using Bayesian Neural Networks for real-world problems often results in computationally expensive predictions due to the necessity of post-processing their outputs to incorporate uncertainty estimation. This study presents an efficient method for computing classification uncertainty on entire datasets, similar to a Monte Carlo approximation. Derived from a theoretical analysis of Bayesian Neural Networks' output distribution, this approach facilitates straightforward extensions to compute uncertainty in features and gradient information. Its utility in relaying classification uncertainty down the pipeline could be beneficial in applications such as astronomical data analysis. The proposed method is also adaptable to more complex scenarios involving data such as spatial points, vectors, or graphs. The presented methodology offers an alternative to relying on noisy data for estimating uncertainty, allowing it to be a supplementary tool for assessing model reliability and making confidence-driven decisions.

Recent studies on Brillouin scattering in 2D materials have largely concentrated on isolated mechanical modes rather than their interactions. A crucial factor influencing these interactions is the type of symmetry mechanical modes adhere to. A phenomenon called intermodal Brillouin interaction occurs when mechanical modes from different symmetries are coupled, and this interaction can be modulated by the inherent characteristics of mechanical modes based on their symmetry. In our investigation, we examined the effects of mechanical symmetry on intermodal Brillouin interactions in a 2D material - hexagonal boron nitride. By utilizing a combination of simulations and measurements, we identified and studied high-order mechanical modes in both radio frequency and optical domains while also observing intermodal Brillouin interactions. A comparison of our experimental results with theoretical predictions confirmed that mechanical parameters can be accurately determined from these interactions. Moreover, fine-tuning mechanical modes to adhere to specific symmetries allowed us to selectively enhance or suppress intermodal Brillouin interactions, thereby offering a versatile way to manage these interactions and accurately measure mechanical parameters.

The general 0-GGS of a finite classical Coxeter group Bn is investigated in this context, with a focus on its exchange laws that aren't governed by the Veech criteria. This study reveals that these alternative exchange laws, limited to moves involving adjacent roots, are constrained by the group's Coxeter length and the elements within its descent set. This finding builds upon prior work by Billera and Postnikov, who analyzed the generalized standard exchange laws in the context of Bn's Coxeter combinatorial fans.

In recent years, a variety of novel mathematical models have been created to optimize the Oil Refining and Transportation Problem, a critical issue in supply chain operations. Two of these models, the Stochastic Uniform Capacitated Plant (SUKP) and the Bi-Modal Community Pickup and Delivery (BMCP) problems, are particularly significant. Researchers have proposed a high-efficiency iterative local search algorithm, E2LS, to address these SUKP and BMCP scenarios. This algorithm uses an equilibrium solution as a starting point to efficiently explore solutions, resulting in a global optimal solution for corresponding linear programming formulations. The E2LS algorithm exhibits a substantial time performance improvement of 43.15% and 67.94% compared to existing methods for SUKP and BMCP, respectively.

In recent years, the task of forecasting customer churn has gained significant interest from businesses seeking to prevent loss and achieve long-term growth. Most effective solutions for churn prediction have been found in complex Artificial Neural Network models. However, these models require considerable time and resources to build and test. The main goal of this research paper is to demonstrate the efficiency of using simple Artificial Neural Networks for churn prediction and forecast based on short-term history, as well as highlight their advantages in terms of speed and ease of use. The study examines how various models perform when trained on different periods of time from the same dataset. It also delves into the efficiency of using Artificial Neural Networks for forecast generation, in addition to predicting churn. The paper is concluded with suggestions for future studies in this field.

It's known that the magnetic irrelevance in the Ising Field Theory makes the effective theory integrable at a very low energy scale due to a non-diagonal operator $L_{-4}{ ar L}_{-4}	heta$. However, after applying real-time evolution induced by $H_{FF}$, a level crossing occurs, leading to a transition in the integrability of the effective theory. Specifically, for the operator $L_{-2}	 ar L_{-2}	heta$, we demonstrate the effective theory's integrability by constructing a local Lax pair. Furthermore, our research reveals that the spin-1/2 compact quantum group symmetry of the Ising Field Theory is preserved in the effective theory at any time.

The lattice calculation of the gluon TMDPDF's soft factor has been analyzed using the method of large $x$ expansion in lattice QCD with a specific emphasis on twisted boundary conditions. A factorization formula was first proposed for the gluon TMDPDF's lattice calculation without boundary conditions, but a new formula has been developed to account for the presence of boundary conditions. Although the new formulas are theoretically similar, they are marked by the presence of a geometric phase associated with the twisted boundary, but only in certain circumstances and with a specific value of momentum. Utilizing a specific mathematical approach called the Bruhat decomposition, the role of the gluon link's high-order perturbation series in the factorization formula was clarified, revealing that the geometric phase plays a significant part in the factorization. Moreover, the geometric phase's presence has been linked to a specific issue related to momentum derivatives in the factorization formula. The new formulas for the lattice calculation of the gluon TMDPDF have been rigorously tested against numerical data obtained from a specific simulation known as the \textit{tram} and a twist-4 gluon condensate calculation under both twisted and periodic boundary conditions.

The underlying physics of electron and positron production in high-energy collisions between heavy nuclei has been the subject of intense research for many years. In this research, we have employed a quantum mechanical and relativistic model of electromagnetic interactions to explain the creation of electron-positron pairs during collisions between heavy nuclei. In our model, we used the Dirac-Coulomb equation to modify the original non-relativistic Coulomb potential into a relativistic one that takes into account the electromagnetic interactions of these particles. By applying this modified potential to both the Schwinger's electromagnetic quantum action principle and a relativistic two-body scattering equation, we have developed two key methods to understand the distribution of these produced electrons and positrons. In the first method, we used the many-body Schrödinger equation to describe this distribution, while in the second, we used the deconstructed scattering equation with a relativistic Coulomb potential. In this research, we have successfully calculated and graphically represented the probability of electron-positron production in gold-gold, lead-lead, and uranium-uranium collisions at specific energies through these models for various values of the coupling parameter. We found that there is both agreement and difference between the probabilities obtained from our two methods, and our results show that the effects of electromagnetic fields on the distribution of these produced particles are very complex, particularly in the strong fields generated during the collision of very heavy nuclei.

The rapidly growing number of urban cyclists makes them a significant group to study in order to improve safety, especially in cities like Amsterdam with its extensive cycling network. By integrating data from various sources, like city data and crowd-sourced monitoring systems, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of cyclists' behavior. However, there is often a limitation to the amount of data available, and it is difficult to determine its accuracy. In this research, we examine the potential of a cycling monitor program as a tool to gather data and improve the city's cycling safety, while also addressing the challenges associated with data collection.

This study introduces a multi-model predictive control framework for robotic path implementation, considering uncertain environmental models and system models. a novel algorithm is proposed to calculate the control input while taking into account multiple potential system models. This approach utilizes the polytopic approximation method for uncertainty analysis and applies the least squares method for parameter identification. a quadratic convex optimization problem is formulated to determine the control input, incorporating constraints for safety, steering, and control input limitations. a case study using a high-precision robotic wheeled vehicle demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm in navigating uncertain environments.

We establish in this paper that the covering number of a ring without unity is equal to the covering number of a unital ring formed by adding an identity element to the ring's products. Consequently, this result provides an equivalence between the covering numbers of a unital ring and its quotient ring. Furthermore, this concept leads to a correction of a previously published finding by the same authors.

It is well known that basic neural networks can be vulnerable to adversarial attacks but it remains unclear if this flaw is inherent in all neural networks. In our research, we investigate the inherent connection between a network's capacity and the capability to form adversarial examples. By using a scenario with specific data distributions and controlled error margins, we created a framework to evaluate a network's robustness. We found that when error margins are restricted to a $0\%+\varepsilon$ threshold, no deep neural network can achieve zero error regardless of its complexity for the scenario we've created. This contradicts the non-adversarial performance, leading to the phenomenon we refer to as the 'adversarial advantage'. Moreover, we developed a new method to generate robust adversarial examples, and the results show that the performance of the model remains consistent even with increased error thresholds, indicating the inherent connection between a network's capacity and robustness.

Recent studies on convolution kernels have demonstrated their effectiveness in obtaining smooth nonlinear diffusion equations. This research investigates a convolution kernel known as the'squared hat kernel,' specifically with an integral of absolute value equal to 2. The paper demonstrates that for a certain class of nonlinear conservation laws, solutions smoothed by this kernel converge to entropy-satisfying solutions under Shizuta-Kowada energy. Furthermore, the smoothed solutions of the diffusion equation and its linear diffusion approximation both converge to the same limit. This smooth diffusion equation is also shown to approximate the original nonlinear conservation law in a suitable functional space with an error rate of 1/2.

We investigate the behavior of hyperbolic closed geodesics in the unit tangent bundle of a hyperbolic manifold. Let TˆT be the iterated tangent structure formed by conjugating the geodesic flow with a suitable deformation, and consider the natural projection map π from the ball TˆT to the unit circle SˆT. Our main finding is that the directions of these geodesics become densely populated on SˆT under a specific condition, which involves the parameters of the manifold. This dense population phenomenon was previously observed by Gurevich, Pansukova, and Schuech for a particular case of a closed hyperbolic surface embedded in higher-dimensional spaces and is now generalized for all types of hyperbolic manifolds.

We have developed a sophisticated approach for non-invasive mapping of the brain's connectivity network. Building on Total Correlation, a correlative time-series analysis method, we've shown its potential to create a six-node connectivity map of the human brain withstanding the challenges of finite sample sizes. To further advance this research, we've established a mathematical framework for determining the underlying parameters of our Total Correlation model when dealing with data series from multiple nodes in a network. We've also found that our model is capable of detecting even subtle alterations in brain connectivity, making it a promising tool for use in both basic research and medical diagnostics as a potential seizure-forecasting or Alzheimer's-disease-diagnostics tool. To illustrate the capabilities of our mathematical framework, we've used computer simulations to demonstrate its applications and benefits.

This paper builds upon the concept of Newton kernels within the context of Clifford algebra-valued functions, extending existing work in [arXiv:1908.08750]. The resulting formulas have applications in $n$-dimensional spaces and cover a range of cases, including cases where $n$ is equal to $2$, $3$, or $4$. The relational structure between these formulas is similar to that observed in the one-dimensional case, as explored in the paper's appendix. The text also outlines practical uses for these formulas in the context of Monte Carlo simulations. The discussion includes an examination of the potentials expressed as singular square-integrable functions and and highlights a notable link to the concept of an operator having no adjoint. For the purposes of Monte Carlo investigations, we focus on scenarios where the operator has an adjoint, before considering the more singular 'riemannian' Newton kernels. The paper concludes with a new interpretation of Clifford algebra-valued functions as square-integrable quantities in an $n+1$-dimensional space. This leads to a set of corresponding gauge fields, which can be applied in both the geometric algebra and Clifford calculus frameworks. The resulting formulas for these gauge fields are presented in both differential and integral form, before exploring the connection to the Dirac equation in its classical form. The paper also explains the underlying principles through the use of analogy and detailed discussion, providing a thorough and complete presentation of the discussed concepts and formulas.

Conditional conditioning on observations within Gaussian processes yields an efficient way to sample posterior distributions by leveraging remaining uncertainties. By utilizing conditional conditioning in conjunction with a pathwise approach, we develop a versatile framework for drawing samples from a range of posterior distributions. Our method employs a set of conditional variance functions, which we determine through a kernel ridge regression analysis. To minimize computational burdens, we solve for these conditional variances in low-dimensional subspaces associated with each sampling point. Ultimately, our approach allows the efficient approximation of posterior distributions in high-dimensional spaces by leveraging the computationally efficient inference of conditional variances at a set of sampling points.

This paper proposes a new model for estimating the power received by ad-hoc communication links between unmanned aerial vehicles and ground-based sensors in urban jungles. The analysis takes into account that these communication paths intersect with those of other vehicles, creating multiple intersecting signals. To address this challenge, we introduce a modified Two-Ray model that initially calculates each vehicle's signal strength and propagation loss, before combining these signals at the receiving device. To validate our approach, we utilize Monte-Carlo simulations to examine the performance of the new model within urban environments. Our results show that the Two-Ray model outperforms the free space model by producing a more conservative estimate of signal strength. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of interference from overlapping signals on the performance of ad-hoc communication systems, including the effects of different modulation rates and the distribution of nodes within the network.

The DUNE experiment's far detector site is located in Mexico, specifically
inside the SURF lab at the former Homestake Mining Company. Due to its
underground location at a depth of 1.5 km below ground, the DUNE far detector
has the potential to detect rare signals such as proton decay as well as other
non-neutrino particles, in addition to its primary goal of studying neutrino
physics. In this study, the expected background rates for various types of
reactions and decays in the DUNE far detector are estimated using current
measures of neutrino cross sections. In particular, the DUNE far detector's
expected background rates for various forms of decay and reactions on
nucleons, nuclei, and other materials, as well as Cosmogenic reactions and
radioactive decays, are given in terms of expected event rates. In addition to
these calculations, the review examines how the DUNE far detector's design
contributes to its ability to detect rare signals such as Cosmogenic events and
proton decay.

The Shapley framework provides a comprehensive understanding of how individual features within a model contribute to its overall performance. Our comprehensive evaluation of Shapley methods reveals the challenges and advantages of eight implementations when applied to machine learning models in various contexts. Our experiments expose coding inefficiencies and mathematical inaccuracies that hamper the performance of some implementations. On datasets of moderate complexity, these issues severely impact training times and the Shapley values computed. Our findings also raise critical concerns about the practical applications of some methods. In contrast, we argue that the partial dependence evaluation approach offers a more realistic and relevant way to assess feature importance.

This work offers a comprehensive framework called VOSS (Virtual Observatory Software Stack) for building, managing, and perpetuating VO services within the astronomical community. A VO service, such as a data reduction software, regulates data access and applies user-selected processing options to returned data. Our approach acknowledges that various interpretations of VO concepts - specifically how they are applied in different contexts - hampers progress in this field. To address this challenge, we created a conceptual layer in VOSS where abstract ideas are defined and made available for implementation by specific services. This layer ensures that user applications interact with well-defined concepts even if the underlying data storage or web service interfaces change. To facilitate progress in VOSS development, we established a process for reviewing and accepting new services without requiring extensive modifications to the framework's core. Additionally, we developed a virtual machine to streamline service deployment and provide a stable operating environment. Our goal is to empower developers to build their services on top of a stable foundation without worrying about core functionality.

Off-policy reinforcement learning can be very efficient but only if the estimation of the target probability density function is accurate. Typically, policy gradient methods assume a probabilistic policy and use data to estimate it. However, most methods struggle with sampling errors because they calculate the policy distribution based on current knowledge, then collect new data which may not reflect the policy at its current best state. This research proposes a probabilistic approach to experience replay by utilizing variance reduction to improve the accuracy of policy gradient estimation without altering the off-policy structure. Furthermore, it is shown that this new approach has a more stable gradient estimation than existing methods and can be directly applied to several well-known reinforcement learning algorithms. Experimental results confirm that this new approach leads to better sample efficiency and performance compared to other state-of-the-art methods.

Utilizing superbosonization, an advanced variation of the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, we establish the symmetries of generalized $U(1)$-symmetric Abelian gauge theories. Our work beautifully showcases the superbosonization formula's comprehensive merger of bosonization and the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation steps. Moreover, we investigate the applications of superbosonization to the perturbative computation of a non-Abelian $SU(N)$ gauge theory's Jacobian, aiming to contribute to a deeper understanding and possibly render non-Abelian quantum electrodynamics' perturbative calculations more manageable.

The Detail Context Block, a proposed module for spatiotemporal learning, has been demonstrated to be highly effective when used as a pre-training strategy for video recognition tasks. By incorporating Detail Context Blocks into a basic 3D CNN model, the model is able to leverage more detailed context information, which in turn enhances its overall performance. Through an exhaustive evaluation of different Detail Context Blocks and unit lengths, the results showed that the Detail Context Block led to a significant 62.25% and 55.52% improvement in 1-shot and 5-shot settings, respectively, for both Epileptic Seizure Detection and Video Object Detection tasks. Additionally, the results indicated that the Detail Context Block was able to reach the state-of-the-art performance without resorting to data augmentation or online data mining. Finally, the experiments demonstrated that the Detail Context Block was able to maintain its high performance even when it was subjected to a significant reduction in resources.

Imperative programs have well-precedented memory pitfalls that can be addressed
by incorporating a type system ensuring memory safety in languages such as
C and C++. A type system for memory management can also be utilized in
object-oriented languages like Java, which has previously lacked such an system
from a type checking perspective. This research presents Essent, a static
analysis system for ensuring memory safety in Java through type checking for
object creation, copying, removal from lists, canonicalization, and garbage
collection. Essent is implemented as a plugin for the Essent language and its
powerful type system, being the first known implementation of such a system
for Java and its patterns of memory management, and it's notable for being
polyvariant, which enables distinct memory management views for distinct program
sections. Essent also offers a type system for data flow properties related to
memory, such as ensuring never-before objects are not given to methods that
free their contents, and that freeed objects are not accessed. Essent's
distinction lies in its type system reasoning capabilities for this specific
problem, and it's solved delving into the what and when of the memory management
process, resulting in a more practical system than just the what.

A sequence of research proposals is presented to verify the existence of heavy neutral leptons using ongoing experiments. These concepts build upon prior work in ar:XV.06475, expanding our current understanding and suggesting new directions for exploration. Heavy neutral leptons have the potential to significantly elevate beyond-the-standard-model lepton flux generated at neutrino experiments, and various research pathways are being developed to verify the existence of this new particle. In a subsequent paper, the feasibility of detecting heavy neutral leptons using lepton colliders will be examined in more detail.

This work introduces an innovative joint decoding approach for pre-transformed polar codes, including variants with CRC checking, by taking advantage of their inherent inner-code dependencies. The proposed method utilises a tree search algorithm to identify the most likely codeword under Bayes assumptions, leveraging a graphical representation of the code to facilitate efficient lookup. In practical applications, the proposed decoding strategy can be seamlessly integrated into existing base codes with minimal additional complexity and hardware requirements. Consequently, the proposed approach yields substantial decoding gains for pre-transformed polar codes when compared to conventional success-oriented and error-correction-oriented techniques. Moreover, the analysis shows that the proposed decoding method can attain near-optimality for a broad range of channel conditions.

Nonlinear coaddition techniques like median and clipped-mean are preferred over linear methods in exoplanet searches due to their ability to eliminate outliers. However, our research reveals that these algorithms fail to maintain a consistent point spread function (PSF) profile, which is essential for accurately measuring relative fluxes between coadded frames. Since astrometric and photometric calculations are based on these relative fluxes, errors arise due to PSF variations. Using real Hubble Space Telescope images, our study demonstrates the significant variations in PSF renormalization coefficients and their impact on astrometric and photometric measurements. Notably, these discrepancies prove to be tenfold larger than those associated with prior threats, including read-thru and write-overwrite errors. Consequently, our findings suggest that nonlinear algorithms should be modified to maintain a consistent PSF profile or else corrected for its effect on the data they produce.

A theoretical approach has been developed to analyze the stability of sharp notches in materials by applying the concepts of sharpening instability to understand how and where cracks initiate. According to a modified version of the linearized Willamowski-Neumann criterion, critical stress concentrations occur in regions where the gradient of the local tangent modulus exceeds a material-dependent threshold. By combining this criterion with a simple model of the notch, researchers have identified two possible locations for the notch tip where instability may occur, leading to an irreversible decrease in the material's strength. By applying this approach to various types of notches, they found that in some cases, both locations are susceptible to sharpening instability, but in other cases, one location is more prone to instability than the other. Furthermore, numerical simulations based on this approach have demonstrated that the location of crack initiation in notches depends on the ratio of the radius of the notch tip to the critical length of the material. These findings have been used to establish a method for determining the critical length of materials by analyzing the shapes of cracks induced in unnotched specimens.

We develop a notion of "imaginary surfaces" to describe self-mapping spaces of the form $\gamma(T)$, where $\gamma$ is a solution to the chordal SLE$_6$ in conformal Euclidean space, and represent the driving function through an operator algebraic framework. Imaginary surfaces can be seen as non-conformal equivalents of hyperbolic buildings' walls in Ptolemaean metric spaces. Utilizing the Loukas-Mier-Ambrosvetisou space and its action on $L^2(\mathbb{H}^2)$, we drive the SLE$_6$ driving function toward convergence within the space. Consequently, the study leads to self-mapping spaces' characterization of $\gamma(T)$ and definition of the Schramm-Loewner evolution's imaginary surfaces. Recent findings on multiple branching SLEs suggest that these imaginary surfaces constitute a comprehensive framework for understanding the multiple branching process in SLE.

This study establishes the existence of strong solutions for the Navier-Stokes equations in a three-dimensional domain for 2019-2020, with specific nonhomogeneous initial conditions. We demonstrate that the solution's maximum derivative values are directly proportional to the maximum derivative values of the initial conditions, using a fixed domain of analysis. Furthermore, the analysis takes into account nonhomogeneous boundary conditions and initial values in both temperature and velocity, while accounting for nonhomogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. A key assumption in this analysis is that the nonhomogeneous boundary conditions satisfy a specific mean value property.

This study introduces a new verifiable learning scheme known as CVQC, for the verification of k-nearest neighbor classification. CVQC is shown to be secure based on the assumption related to a specific type of quantum homomorphic evaluation, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through a comparison of its computation and verification times to existing methods. Notably, the verification time of CVQC is significantly faster, with a significantly smaller public key size as well. A CVQC implementation using the Theia quantum library on a Microsoft quantum development kit demonstrated verification times of 15 microseconds and 5.8 microseconds for single and dual quantum input scenarios respectively, resulting in a speedup of 9.52 and 11.35 times over the fastest existing method for dual inputs.

Integrating blockchain technology into supply chain management enables the creation of a distributed ledger, ensuring that all transactions are valid and unalterable. However, the high energy consumption of existing consensus algorithms has significant financial implications and hinders the scalability of blockchain-based applications. To mitigate this issue, we have developed a novel LC4IoT consensus mechanism tailored for IoT settings, characterized by low energy consumption and high throughput. The LC4IoT consensus relies on a voting system, incorporating a compact round-digest and proof-of-work to ensure validity and prevent 51% attacks. The mechanism leverages the LC4IoT consensus to achieve low energy consumption, enabling the creation of a decentralized distributed ledger. We have formulated and mathematically proven the LC4IoT consensus as an optimization problem to ensure it follows blockchain properties. The LC4IoT consensus is designed to be compatible with a variety of blockchain networks and can be applied to real-world settings without further modification. Moreover, our approach enables the selection of the most suitable consensus algorithm for a given application. To verify the performance of the LC4IoT consensus, we have conducted a numerical analysis and experimentally validated its efficiency and throughput in a real-world setting.

Despite significant advancements in image analysis, accurate cell shape, tracking, and
segmentation prove notoriously difficult, partly due to the complexity and variability of cells.
This study leverages deep generative models for synthetic cell shape creation, and uses these shapes
in a simulated environment to develop a template-based method for automatic cell segmentation.
By training a radio-guided generative adversarial model, we can generate numerous tailored shapes
that match a target cell and apply it to an image analysis task. Our results demonstrate that our
approach compares favorably to state-of-the-art methods for cell segmentation, and we believe that
our work will facilitate the development of more robust image analysis tools, particularly in
cell tracking.

This research paper seeks to address the navigation challenge within complex scientific documents for visually impaired individuals. Despite existing technologies that enable the fixation detection and attention analysis in healthy vision, our focus lies on developing a fixation prediction and identification method for large-scale internal object targets within document pages. The proposed system employs computer vision techniques to achieve this goal. Evaluation was conducted on the 'Eye To The Future' dataset and two baseline models were analyzed for accuracy. The study found that the predictive results of the vision-based approaches were comparable to those of deep learning models on fixation prediction tasks and outperformed them in identifying the location of each fixation. The findings demonstrate that vision-based techniques can effectively support navigation in documents, thereby improving the overall reading experience for individuals who are print-disabled.

BERT has shown exceptional performance in Natural Language Processing and related areas, but it has limitations due to its restriction to pre-trained datasets. A new model, called XLNet, uses the Extended Self-Attention mechanism to overcome this limitation and achieve better performance than BERT models in various tasks, while also being more efficient. We found that implementing XLNet on a GPU using tensor-coordinates can lead to significant speed improvements of at least 40%, allowing it to match the performance of a CPU-based implementation. We also discovered that using half-precision floating-point numbers in the forward pass doesn't affect the model's performance, resulting in a 50% reduction in the number of floating-point operations. Notably, these optimizations enabled us to win first prize in the NLP challenge at Kaggle, and we learned that tensor coordinates can be beneficial in other models as well.

Determining the structure and population parameters of binary star systems relies heavily on determining their component properties, especially their masses and luminosities. Since mass is tied to size and luminosity, it's essential to have accurate measurements of these parameters. Recent advancements in spectroscopy and astrometry have improved the detection of binary systems, especially small ones, which have shifted the focus from system masses below one solar mass. Here we discuss the role of high-resolution spectroscopy in characterizing these binary systems by determining their component specific parameters.

In a first for its kind, the Keck/LRS spectrometer was used to observe Taurus binary systems at high resolution. This was achieved by utilizing a specially developed algorithm to combine the velocities of a large sample of stellar cross-correlation, which yielded precise radial velocities. Additionally, the spectrometer was tested for its accuracy using a reference list of binary systems in the Taurus region, which further refined the velocities of these systems.

The study found that high-resolution spectroscopy plays a key role in understanding the effects of stellar contamination as opposed to actual planetary signals. It's essential to understand the cross-correlation properties of stellar spectra to determine population parameters in binary systems. By analyzing the cross-correlation properties of spectra from the Taurus region, the spectrometer was able to identify potential sources of contamination and mark them for further study.

Given its improved performance, the cross-correlation method has become a valuable tool for determining the parameters of binary systems in the Taurus region.

We classify constant curvature metrics on the $2k$ dimensional sphere with conical singularities isometrically embedded in $\mathbb{H}^{2k}$ to hyperbolic space. These metrics are extensions of a previously classified case with a single singularity. Our work also implies a second application: it categorizes hyperbolic metrics on the Riemann sphere with conical singularities and real hypermultiplet weights, which are connected to the classification of $N=2$ supergravity solutions of the conformal to the Ayler-MacKay metric, a specific case of the Wigner metrics, already known and not appearing in the literature.

The classic argument that living organisms benefit from fluid dynamics through reduced drag does not entirely apply, with evidence suggesting that fluid forces can also hinder movement. A recent study published in Nature Communications explored how the interplay between fluid forces and a living organism's movement influences their overall behavior. To address this, researchers analyzed the locomotion strategies of the Centipede, Illepidophorus, which swims using a unique tail motion. By combining computational and analytical models, they found that this behavior allows the Centipede to avoid being pulled apart by fluid forces. When testing the Centipede's locomotion strategy in a linear environment, the results showed that fluid forces can either aid or hinder its movement, with an observed maximum speed occurring at a specific Reynolds number. A theoretical model based on phase space was also developed and confirmed to describe the Centipede's motion accurately. Comparing the effects of fluid forces on the Centipede to those of inertia, the findings suggested that fluid forces can either aid or cost the Centipede speed, depending on its swimming pattern and the surrounding fluid environment. Therefore, this study suggests that fluid forces can have a complex impact on living organisms, influencing their movement in a non-intuitive manner.

A proposed hybrid approach, dubbed Adaptive Simulation, allows a single simulation with multiple code branches to efficiently navigate the complex spatial gradients from deep ocean to land intrusion during a tsunami. This method leverages the speed of weakly nonlinear shallow water equations in the open ocean with the ability to run parallel code branches that progressively incorporate more accurate Navier-Stokes equations as the water depth decreases. As the simulation nears the shore, where fluid non-slippage conditions apply, the Navier-Stokes equations take over, and the branches merge to solve the more computationally intensive tasks. A series of simulations conducted in the Pacific, ranging from Hawaii to California, demonstrated a 3.5-fold increase in efficiency compared to a non-adaptive method, with results that were virtually indistinguishable upon visual inspection. An additional experiment was also undertaken to refine the solution near the shore of the Hawaiian Islands, achieving a 5.3-fold increase in accuracy in tsunami wave amplitudes in the nearshore zone.

Detecting highly massive galaxies at very high redshifts is vital for completing the cosmic census during the reionization era. To investigate the evolution of the most massive galaxies of elite stature, we employed the near-infrared spectrograph IRDC18b on the Ukidss to identify and study a highly massive galaxy at z=4.23. By taking advantage of the wide instrumental base of Ukidss, we successfully retrieved the spectrum of a highly massive galaxy, namely HD13dsm24c, which has a star formation rate of 40+-13 Msol/yr. The spectrum of HD13dsm24c indicates a redshift of 4.23, consistent with our selection method that avoids using emission lines. In doing so, we've successfully identified the first report of a galaxy with a strong 1.56 micron absorption feature via Ukidss's wide instrumental base. By using a likelihood ratio method, we've obtained a signal to noise ratio of 21 at 1.56 micron, second only to QSOs. The spectrum of HD13dsm24c indicates a similar nature to very massive galaxies at z=4.7-5.5 via JWST's emission line selection. Our selection criteria are highly efficient with an estimated 90% effectiveness when using a 1.56 micron absorption feature and a noise limit of 20 sigma within a field of view of 0.66 square degrees. We have developed a seven-dimensional gravity framework that can yield a range of
rotating AdS7 spaces, including spaces with SU(4) symmetry. These solutions can be
characterized by a non-compact spin 1 field. A specific solution with SO(4) symmetry,
corresponding to a charged D7-brane probe, has also been found and analyzed.

The study of disc jamming in complex two-dimensional spaces has been explored using a cellular robotic system called Polaris. By confining the discs within a 7x7 grid of cells, researchers replicated known effects of weight and size on jamming, including the propensity for heavier discs to jam more easily and larger discs to outshine smaller ones in the grid's center. Additionally, an algorithm was applied to the system to assess jamming as a local property and further tests were conducted to examine how the distribution of disc sizes influences system jamming.

Recent research suggests that various types of El Ni\~no (EN) and La Ni\na\ (LN) events may contribute to increased climate variability and risk assessment difficulties. To address this challenge, a comprehensive set of Sobol' sensitivity indices has been employed to investigate the impact of EN/LN types on Chinese precipitation patterns. To facilitate this analysis, a novel hybrid approach combining GM(1) and ADO methods was developed to parameter space exploration, using multiple-objective optimization to determine the optimal parameters for a grey-Bernoulli-Bernoulli (GBB) system based on time series lengths and correlation coefficients. This hybrid approach allowed for the efficient optimization of parameters and the calculation of sensitivity indices, effectively utilizing grey system data to develop novel statistical methods for identifying EN/LN types based on multiple precipitation patterns. The results showed that the proposed method successfully detected and differentiated between different types of precipitation patterns, accurately identified from a theoretical perspective, and also recovered the known precipitation patterns of the GBB model. Furthermore, the predicted precipitation patterns from the optimized GBB model exhibited high correspondence with the actual precipitation patterns, and the first two elements of the state vector in the GBB model displayed consistent differentiation between the EN/LN types.

Nonaffine behavior within the elastic range of disordered materials remains uncontroversially present, however its manifestation is still challenging to verify through experimental evidence. Nonaffinity's presence can be validated by measuring the angle between the force displacement curve and the linear, ideal energy storage line drawn after a prolonged, thermodynamic relaxation process. Our research introduces an energy-optimal, maximally linear relation known as the "ML-line", which can be estimated through a simple analysis or computed directly using a material's force-relaxation data. By comparing the ML-line with the actual, thermodynamically relaxed energy storage line, the angle between these two, ideal and real, lines can be used to quantify the extent of nonaffine behavior within a material. Our research demonstrates the convergence of the ML-line and the actual energy storage lines for increasingly long, pre-rheological relaxation times, where the exponent underlying these converging lines is found to be 1.5 in the case of the widely studied and commonly used standard linear hard-sphere model. Additionally, the simplicity and insensitivity of the ML-line to various time scales, which dictate a material's affine behavior, make it an analytically and experimentally useful metric for gauging nonaffinity within disordered materials, such as soft and biological materials, which are characterized by multiple time scales.

This paper examines the collection of SIS models as a whole, focusing on how these models evolve over time and whether they have stable equilibrium states. By utilizing an operator representation of the SIS model, it is demonstrated that the characteristics of these models not only depend on the rate at which new individuals join the susceptible population but also on the random events that occur independently of this rate. In a comparative study of different single-population models with varying degrees of stochastic activity, it was revealed that the level of these random events has a significant impact on the existence of stable equilibrium states in each model. This analysis also enables a broader understanding of the SIS model by framing the probability of random events as a second rate parameter.

This study investigates the computational requirements of fuzzy logic models in multi-variable temporal logic, specifically when dealing with a single variable. Firstly, we demonstrate the capability of fuzzy Bounded Labeled Transition Systems to model and evaluate fuzzy logic formulas with degree of truth expressed using the real numbers. We then outline a method for automatically generating a fuzzy Bounded LTL using a saturation algorithm, resulting in a decision procedure of unspecified complexity. We further propose a reduction from fuzzy Bounded LTL to a restricted version with low-complexity transition systems, yielding a semi-decision procedure of unspecified complexity. We provide a comparative analysis of the achieved complexity bounds with those of classical LTL, showing that adding fuzzy elements does not elevate the complexity beyond what is already known for classical logic. Additionally, we provide a method for automatically generating a fuzzy logic model based on a given fuzzy transition system, along with a associated decidability proof.

One critical issue in social media monitoring involves maintaining comprehensive and precise taxonomy systems containing relevant terms to track online discussions. Social media analytics requires an automatic process to continuously update and enlarge taxonomies to capture emerging social topics. The existing research focuses on selecting relevant synonyms from concept networks like WordNet, yet it is impractical to repeatedly access and process the network for each taxonomy expansion operation. Additionally, previous studies commonly utilized techniques such as lexical ontologies, ontological relationships, co-occurring terms, question answer datasets and crowdsourcing. In this research, we present a novel taxonomy expansion approach that efficiently balances thoroughness and efficiency in finding suitable synonyms. The proposed HyperExpan algorithm swiftly identifies relevant synonyms using hypernyms from concept networks like WordNet, while our experimental findings reveal that it achieves up to a 95.7% reduction in cost and outperforms the standard synonyms in precision, requiring significantly fewer search and match operations.

A thorough examination was conducted to evaluate the performance of density functional approximations in predicting the electric dipole autoconvolution, electric dipole moment distribution, and electric absorption of molecular dimers. Ten DFT models, including five commonly used DFT methods paired with six density functional approximations, were employed to achieve these goals. The outcomes showed that certain DFT methods and functionals can effectively predict the autoconvolution and moment distribution of dimers with high accuracy. However, the outcomes varied greatly in predicting the electric absorption. Our results indicate that the Piobeta* model consistently outperformed the other functional in predicting the autoconvolution, moment distribution, and electric absorption. The outcomes also highlight the significant influence of the orientation of the monomers in the dimer on the predictive strength of the methods. This study serves as a useful reference for researchers in choosing appropriate methods for predicting the electric properties of molecular dimers.

Combining non-stochastic and probabilistic uncertainty modeling enhances the capabilities of industrial systems for handling uncertainty. A novel framework, the Continuous-Time Markov Chain Linear Quadratic Regulator with Stochastic Disturbances (CT-MCLQRs-S), is developed to address this combination. This framework models a system's dynamics as CT-MCLQRs and incorporates the state transition probabilities of a continuous-time Markov chain to represent Markovian uncertainties. An optimization method for calculating the CT-MCLQRs-S controller is presented using the algebraic CT-MCLQRL method and a probabilistic version of the algebraic Riccati equation. CT-MCLQRs-S is demonstrated in a real-world application to a two-stage continuous system with a Markovian uncertainty and a mixed non-deterministic and stochastic uncertainty in a three-stage discrete system, showing its effectiveness in achieving optimal performance.

Quantitative system design focuses on creating detailed specifications that incorporate performance and reliability metrics, enabling the evaluation of performance and reliability through analysis and simulation before and during system operation.  This paper examines the process of mapping high-level performance and reliability requirements into resilient system designs.  A novel approach to performance and reliability assessment is presented, based on a specific method of Durability and Recoverability measurement called the Resilience Satisfaction Value (ReSV).  This measurement breaks down specifications into manageable parts and assigns weights to each part, ultimately providing a comprehensive analysis of a system's performance and reliability.  System designers can use the ReSV metric to identify areas for improvement, optimize these systems for optimal performance and reliability, and assess their resilience in the face of failure, using the ReSV metric to measure performance and reliability in tandem.  Several case studies are included to illustrate the value of the ReSV metric in performance and reliability assessment.

Despite its potential impact, research on dark matter remains limited due to a lack of suitable experimental searches. Conventional approaches face significant challenges related to costs, which is why the use of existing public monitoring systems could provide a key pathway to discovery. Our proposed research involves leveraging a large dataset from global commercial devices, including IoT devices, to create a comprehensive dataset for analyzing dark matter signals. We are developing a monitoring system based on the Dark Matter Statistical Analysis Model (DM-SAM) that utilizes machine learning to identify dark matter-related events in IoT sensor readings. By leveraging this system, users can contribute to the first large-scale search for dark matter utilizing IoT data.

We examine a nonlinear diffusion equation $\partial_t u = \nabla \cdot (|x|^\beta \nabla u^p)$ in the exterior of a bounded smooth domain, with a power function $u \mapsto u^p$ and exponent $\beta > 0$. The equation has a nonzero and smooth solution within a bounded and smooth domain, with the estimate $\|u(t)\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}$ bounded over a finite time interval $[0,T]$. This estimate is an extension of a previous result from Daskalopoulos and P. M. Lee for a related equation with $\beta = 1$. When considering the case where the equation has a nonzero and smooth solution in the entire space $\mathbb{R}^m$, with the estimate $\|u(t) - U\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^m)}$ bounded over a finite time interval $[0,T]$. This estimate is an extension of a previous result from C. M. Dafermos and P. M. Lee for a related equation with $\beta = 1$.

The correlation between the curvature of the low-frequency radio spectrum and polarization of distant radio sources is demonstrated through analysis of data from the Murchison Widefield Intensity Mapping experiment. By comparing polarized counts from the Large Survey Area with the all-sky polarization catalog of CATSGR, a strong relationship between spectrum curvature and polarization is found, showing significant correlation at high polarization levels. The relationship between spectrum curvature and polarization is statistically confirmed and can be described by a low-frequency peak followed by a high-frequency plateau. The measured correlation is seen to occur at a 3σ confidence level, however it is observed that only a small fraction of radio sources correspond to the highest polarization levels, indicating that extragalactic background polarization is mainly caused by a small group of bright radio sources. The findings also suggest that future measurements of the curvature-polarization function could be made with significantly lower statistical errors using only half of the data currently available.

Quantum systems employ entropy to gauge uncertainty, and several notions exist, including classical, quantum, min- and max-entropy. However, beyond abstract principles, specific operational meanings and mathematical formulations of these entropies remain unclear. Conversely, operational concepts like operational differential privacy and information reconciliation are rooted in uncertainty, specifically using max-entropy, but the link between this concept and other entropies remains unclear. To address this gap, a method is proposed to correlate various entropy forms by establishing a unified relationship between them. This is achieved through a concept of equivalence in statistical testing, allowing max-entropy to be defined in terms of min-entropy, and vice versa. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that max-entropy is a more effective measure of uncertainty in certain applications, and that min-entropy is a better choice in others. To illustrate these claims, applications of min-entropy in physics, computer science, and engineering are presented, and potential benefits of using max-entropy in these fields are also explored.

A novel theoretical framework has been developed to study and compare different turbulent transport processes in momentum, heat, and momentum. This framework theory asserts that the turbulent transport operator in a given medium can be expressed as a correlation between the velocity field auto-correlation and the specific characteristics of the medium. Utilizing this concept, we have derived mathematical expressions that describe turbulent transport in both similar and dissimilar coordinate systems. Furthermore, we have applied the framework theory to study and compare turbulent transport in both similar and dissimilar coordinate systems, with a focus on the parallel and perpendicular components of the velocity field. Our findings indicate that the turbulent transport in a given medium can be expressed as a combination of the parallel and perpendicular components. In the case of a Karman street, for example, we have found that the turbulent transport is primarily controlled by the parallel component in a narrow region and the perpendicular component in a broader region. Our research suggests that the parallel component is more effective in a tight vortex structure, whereas the perpendicular component is more effective in a broad vortex structure. In a comparative study on the turbulent transport of momentum and heat, we have found that the turbulent transport of heat is primarily controlled by the parallel component, whereas the turbulent transport of momentum is a balance of the parallel and perpendicular components. Our research suggests that the turbulent transport of heat is a more complex phenomenon than previously thought. Conventional approaches to analyzing elastic scattering data face significant challenges due to their sensitivity to parameters. Global analyzes using phenomenological models can help mitigate this issue but require careful initial assessments. An alternative strategy for overcoming these limitations involves employing reaction models to fit elastic scattering data and calculate essential parameters such as the diffractive slope parameter (B34) without relying on phenomenological models. This study uses the Glauber model to derive an analytical expression for B34 in terms of the density distribution and reaction model parameters, enabling precise extraction of parameters through reaction model-based fits to multiple data sets. Notably, this method results in consistent parameter sets that can be used to determine the optical potential for diffraction dissociation, observables like the real part of the Coulomb amplitude, and the blackening parameter, all of which can be used to predict various experimental outcomes including high-energy optical potentials, DD cross sections, electromagnetic properties of the overlap, and even optical potential parameters before the first minimum. An additional outcome of this method involves obtaining the mean and deviation of mean values for the radii of the density distributions R2, R2+2, etc. for the overlap and for the entire surface including the Blackening parameter.

In the context of blackbody thermodynamics, we reexamine Planck's derivation in a 3D non-magnetic conductor slab under the influence of perfect electric conductivity boundary conditions. This scenario necessitates a revised understanding of thermodynamic quantities because they are no longer free from external influence. Utilizing a mode decomposition of the electromagnetic field, we establish a higher-order expression for the occupation number, which is based on dispersion relations and resonant modes within the slab. As the occupation number displays multi-valued behavior, we address this complexity by identifying the relevant domain and turning point analysis. Notably, our results are in alignment with the research conducted by Landau, Verdet, and Devaux among others. Additionally, we propose an alternative perspective on these findings.

The demand for maintaining user privacy while utilizing location-based services has led to the development of several privacy-preserving models over the years. These models typically focus on safeguarding individual privacy, but there is a growing concern for preserving the privacy of the data itself. Previous approaches have yielded subpar results as they fail to sufficiently address privacy loss, particularly when dealing with data that is conditionally dependent. This work aims to bridge the gap between model privacy and data privacy by proposing a novel framework that utilizes the concept of $q$-Entropic Privacy, leveraging $q$-Entropy metrics for both model parameters and data. The proposed approach consists of two primary components: 1) a mechanism for generating private data through a maximum entropy distribution; 2) a system for counting the occurrence of events in an anonymous manner. Experimental results show that the proposed framework is capable of achieving a high level of data privacy, while maintaining an acceptable level of model accuracy. Furthermore, the framework allows for balancing between model accuracy and data privacy, and it is capable of achieving theoretical levels of information removal while maintaining a reasonable computational cost for generating private data.

Our solution to the Obersthuber Challenge involves implementing a novel place
recognition system that leverages signed distance fields to represent 3D point clouds.
By utilizing a geometric descriptor based on a mesh geometry representation,
we achieve improved efficiency in place recognition compared to previous methods.
Key to our approach is the geometric descriptor's capability to effectively capture
places with various geometries at a lower computational cost, whereas point cloud
descriptors are more prone to noise and distortion. Furthermore, we enhance the
robustness of our system against camera noise and distortion by preprocessing
the distance field before extraction of the geometric descriptor. As a result, we
recorded a 99% accuracy in finding the target distance field among competing sets,
and ultimately successfully identified the target place among various datasets.

Advancements in neuroimaging technologies allow researchers to make new discoveries about the human brain at a functional and structural level. To make the most of these breakthroughs, advanced statistical tools are required for analyzing the complex brain networks they produce. One key task that these tools must perform is calculating the degree of connectivity between brain sites across different individuals to help researchers uncover the brain's network properties and variations. We propose a family of statistical models that measure the connectivity between brain sites across different individuals to help researchers uncover the brain's network properties and variations. These models can be used for a broad range of statistical analysis, including identifying the most effective parameters for creating a reliable map of the brain's functional connectivity. Our results show that considering inter-site effects is crucial for accurately comparing groups of individuals and that our method performs better than existing models.

In this paper, we explore fundamental computational issues - naming and counting - within the scope of a distributed communication system consisting of a group of basic computational stations lacking internal memory facilities in a sequential access mode. We present a straightforward, sequential algorithm for a standard version of the naming problem, along with an in-depth analysis of its computational efficiency characteristics. We also examine the counting problem, which is a variation of the naming problem involving the communication of an integer value from a single station to all others. We offer two distinct solutions for the counting problem: a straightforward approach requiring a specific number of steps proportional to the value to be transmitted and another with a fixed execution time independent of the value. All of our proposed solutions are tailored to a distributed system with a sequential access mode and are thus suitable for a broader range of applications. We assess our algorithms in terms of their computational efficiency, particularly with regard to time and data processing, and confirm that the results are consistent with existing research findings. Additionally, we compare our algorithms to previously suggested solutions for the naming problem. Note that the naming problem has also been studied in a distributed system with a parallel access mode, resulting in more efficient algorithms exhibiting a linear time complexity. However, the variants of the counting problem studied in those settings do not allow for a fixed execution time independent of the value to be transmitted.

To effectively handle the complex code-mixed languages found in data streams, a position-based encoding approach is introduced. This method includes two key components: a new tokenization technique called CMPT, and an encoding method that utilizes relative distances. The position-based encoding can be incorporated into existing sequential language models, enhancing their performance in generating accurate code-mixed text. The proposed system achieves state-of-the-art results on three diverse code-mixed datasets across multiple languages, surpassing previous state-of-the-art models by a significant margin in all instances.

The presence of hydrogen in two different valence states within H$_{3}$S creates a significant band gap, but this condition is met with opposition from the material's high reactivity. The compound's stability under high-pressure conditions has led scientists to investigate its superconducting properties. Recent research has focused on isolating the contribution of quantum metrology from diverse isotope variations, thereby allowing for a more in-depth comparison between theoretical and experimental results. Theoretical research indicates that at room pressure, the coefficient for quantum metrology contributed by two distinct hydrogen isotopes in H$_{3}$S is approximately 0.35, however this value diminishes to 0.23 at 250 GPa. The reduction in the coefficient's value can be attributed to changes in the electron-proton mass ratio resulting from altered electron configuration. The predictions made here can be verified through further calculation and measurement of isotope effects, thereby shedding more light on the compound's quantum properties.

Active vision systems utilizing movement have a restriction on generating motion plans due to limited field of view and sensor capabilities. Cluttered environments make it difficult for the system to plan its motion, while sensor movements can create inconsistent equations that fail to converge to the solution, resulting in an unsolvable problem. To overcome this challenge, we present a new method for generating spatial constraints that utilizes a graph representation to guide motion planning, thereby reducing computation complexity and time. By expanding the search space with possible targets, even with an unsolvable set of constraints, we can achieve efficient motion planning. We accomplished this feat by applying the A* algorithm with the novel constraints, and our results show that the proposed approach works effectively in various environments, surpassing the performance of existing algorithms.

We introduce a novel method for learning-based, sham-less, and weak-pipe camera pose estimation. Our approach incorporates a lightweight, weakly-pipe camera reprojector, which significantly improves pose estimation results in challenging environments. By integrating a learned descriptor with a novel camera model, we enable more accurate predictions of image features, substantially enhancing camera pose estimation performance. Our method also enables the use of various feature extractors and camera reprojectors without necessitating additional training, allowing for increased flexibility and effectiveness. Our experiments using the LineMOD dataset confirm that our approach consistently outperforms existing camera pose estimation techniques, particularly in situations involving heavily occluded objects.

This research focuses on a MIMO interference channel with multiple users and multiple transceiver pairs, where each transmitter and receiver forms a pair and exchanges data. Given the pairs' desire to maximize their individual throughput, we cast this as a optimization problem with a non-standard dual structure. To tackle this challenge, we employ a group LASSO-based approach for parameter estimation at the receiver and propose two algorithms - a standard iterative LASSO algorithm and an accelerated first-order method - for both linear and log-scale objective functions. To illustrate the efficacy of our approach, we verify that it yields better results through simulations outperformed by a few established baselines.

In this study, we investigate the concept of finite harmonic mappings ($K^\circ\to L^\circ$)$ through the lens of symbolic power theory, where the underlying fields are of infinite precision. Here, the pull-back of a rational function semifield is defined for a finite harmonic mapping, but in general, it does not extend to the full rational function domain. However, we demonstrate that symbolic power theory yields an explicit formula for the pull-back of a rational function in terms of a harmonic mapping. Additionally, this method allows us to prove a Capelli formula for linear systems on tropical curves and to compute the tropical Bertini theorem in the presence of a finite harmonic mapping.

This research ensures the existence of a unique quasi-stationary distribution for a Markov process with continuous state spaces and demonstrates that quasi-stationary stationary distributions are exactly the invariant stationary distributions among all quasi-stationary distributions. Additionally, we prove that a certain Markov process meets a specific geometric condition under certain conditions, leading to exponential convergence towards a quasi-stationary distribution. Furthermore, our study provides a way to approximate the transition probability function of a quasi-stationary Markov process using quasi-stationary distributions without knowledge of the memory structure of the process. We also show that the speed of convergence towards a quasi-stationary distribution can be estimated based on certain conditions related to the process' characteristics and the quasi-stationary distribution itself. This research was motivated by a model related to the lifetime of TV receivers.

Building on the findings of Arunav Guha, Ryan Lin, and Jonathan Westen, we demonstrate that integrating specific cocycles leads to the derivation of established and novel knot invariants. This process involves integrating a particular 2-form derived from the Chern-Weil formalism, alongside a cocycle derived from the bicharacteristic Liouville integration method in differential geometry, as described by MacGregor. Furthermore, the results obtained align with those presented in a recent study by the present author, who explored the relationship between Liouville form-based cocycles in de Rham cohomology and knot invariants. It was demonstrated there that integrating specific Liouville forms yields the derivatives of the Kontsevich link invariant and the Fukaya-Moroshov index, as calculated in a Chern-Simons theory framework. Notably, the results presented here offer an alternative explanation, rooted in geometry, of the polynomial properties of these invariants.

We present a novel method to study nematic and superconducting orders in
irrep-specific momentum spaces using a material fixed NMR detector.
Magnetic and resistive transitions in NaFeAs and Na$_{0.8}$FeAs reveal that
nematic fluctuations in LiFeAs and NaFeAs are comparable, whereas superconducting
gap ratios for these materials yield values of 2.1$\pm$0.1 and 1.6$\pm$0.1,
respectively. Notably, our findings for Na$_{0.8}$FeAs and LiFeAs suggest that
nematic fluctuations in 117122 family of materials can be tuned by sodium
concentration. Furthermore, we demonstrate that in NaFeAs, the irreps of $A_{1g}$
and $B_{1g}$ contribute equally to superconducting and nematic orders, and we
estimate the critical temperatures for $d_{x^2-y^2}$ and $\Delta_{5}$ channels to
be $\Theta_{SC}^{d}=6.5 \pm 1$ K and $\Theta_{SC}^{\Delta_5}=3.8 \pm
1$ K, respectively.

A universal constraint is applied to Type-II two Higgs doublet models to ensure compliance with theoretical standards in the Higgs potential and electroweak symmetry breaking. This in turn imposes a universal constraint on the Type-II model's parameter space which can be compared with experimental findings in the mass distribution of the Stueckelberg pseudoscalar. The analysis shows that the majority of the Stueckelberg mass range can be achieved without significant impact on the Higgs and gauge boson masses. However, precise measurements of the Higgs couplings at the future proton collider CERN CMS can verify the Type-II model's assumptions if it generates pseudoscalar masses less than 440 GeV. Nevertheless, the pseudoscalar mass range of 440-770 GeV can only be validated with high confidence at the future proton collider CERNO using specific search methods for the gluon-fusion associated production of the Higgs boson. These studies can be further enhanced with the implementation of an additional CP-odd scalar coupling to fermions. The analysis shows that the main contributions to the production and detection of the Higgs boson originate from its fusion with gluons as well as the decay of the top quark. This in turn enables researchers to conduct the most effective detection searches for the Stueckelberg pseudoscalar at the future proton collider CERNO using top quark final states.
