Although RNNs can effectively predict the next action using previous context information, their performance is hindered when the input video sequence contains occlusions or errors. This limitation causes inaccurate predictions as the occluded region's characteristics are unknown. This paper presents a novel Co-occurrence Action Parsing (CAP) approach addressing this shortcoming by identifying action occurrences and leveraging contextual relationships between adjacent actions to generate parsing tables. In comparison to previous methods, CAP enhances the accuracy of action segmentation and parsing, and also increases recognition accuracy when applied to RNN-based action recognition systems. Experimental findings demonstrate CAP's superiority over other action parsing methods in the UCF-101 Action Parsing Dataset. Further evaluation of CAP is conducted on the UCF-101 and HMDB-51 Datasets for action recognition, showing CAP can elevate the accuracy of RNN-based systems by up to 6%.

The relative occurrences of how $ \Lambda_b^0 $ particles fall apart into other subatomic particles can be calculated using theoretical models and estimated with the aid of data from $ \sqrt{s} $ = 13 TeV $ pp $ collisions collected by the LHCb experiment. Analyzing these processes helps researchers understand the interactions inside b quarks and allows for the evaluation of different theoretical models, such as the standard model of particle physics.

Automated grading systems play a significant role in evaluating student codes for short in-class assignments, providing instant feedback and weights that help determine final exam scores. Despite their importance, few studies have focused on the effectiveness of instant feedback provided by these systems. We used two tools to provide code-grade feedbacks to students in a software engineering course and distributed them via Learning Management Systems (LMS). We conducted a survey to understand students' preferences for these feedback tools and gathered data on student performance, including code coverage and grades. Our results indicate that students who received code coverage feedback performed better in code coverage (11.7%) and grades (3.6%) compared to those who received grade feedback. Additionally, most students preferred code coverage feedback over grade feedback. We found that students who prefer code coverage feedback demonstrate better performance, and we identify potential reasons for this disparity. We suggest incorporating code coverage feedback as a means to improve student performance, and provide recommendations for integrating this feedback into existing grading practices.

Unquipped domain adaptation techniques usually need source data, but in practice, obtaining such data can be difficult and costly. This study presents a new approach called target-aware domain adaptation that performs well without source data. By developing features that work well on the target data distribution, and selecting features that are relevant to the target labels, the approach achieves high classification performance. The results show that our method consistently works better than other domain adaptation methods and feature selection methods in various scenarios. Additionally, we propose a target-driven feature selection method that works better than existing methods by extracting features that are relevant to the target labels. The performance of our method is verified using four real-world datasets.

A nuclear reactor's gas core design's operational parameters are being investigated, with an emphasis on finding the pressure at which it reaches peak efficiency. Using an iterative approach based on the Frank-Kachenov equation, we derived a mathematical expression for determining the critical pressure, and then applied the principle of thermodynamic stability to identify stable and unstable regions within the reactor's interior. We utilized the Frank-Kachenov equation's solution for thermal conductance in conjunction with an optimized Monte Carlo simulation to generate a 3D heat transfer model for the reactor's core, and finally, by analyzing the distribution of energy release sites and fuel particles, we determined the reaction zone thickness and assessed the reactor's efficiency under stable and unstable conditions.

We suggest incorporating a physical embedding layer at the beginning of a neural network to address key challenges in applying deep learning to experimental particle physics. This includes representing variables from detector-based instruments and accounting for their uncertainties, as well as identifying and handling rare events that involve substantial background noise. The proposed embedding layer utilizes existing knowledge of the detector to build representations of its components, which are then combined into a comprehensive event representation that can be processed by a deep belief network to generate an event classification. The objective is to determine whether a deep neural network can effectively capitalize on detector expertise, particularly in the context of the SHiP experiment's challenging task of identifying the existence of very weakly interacting particles such as the Hidden Sector Higgs boson.

In the research, an extensive examination of various atmospheric models for exoplanets and stars called Ultra-Hot Jupiters and M-dwarfs is presented. We analyzed how different models involving the thermosphere of M-dwarf HD 192738 using atmospheric escape theory were affected by two distinct sets of emission data for titanium oxide. However, we couldn't conclude whether our observations of the white light continuum provided insight into the electron density in the upper atmosphere of HD 192738 due to the lack of precise data on the spectrum of this specific star. We were unable to verify the models involving an escape mechanism called hydrodynamic and instead found that a model without this mechanism provided a better fit to the observations, which included data from two telescopes, the Very Large Telescope and the Hubble Space Telescope. However, both models assumed a certain amount of energy and momentum was transferred to the upper atmosphere from the upper stratosphere, which was then lost to space.

This paper offers an in-depth explanation of how logic programs are processed in Answer Set Programming, focusing on the details of grounding algorithms. We provide a comprehensive overview of how the standard procedures operate, whether dealing with recursive or non-recursive logic programs, and whether aggregates are present or absent. The latter factor is particularly significant, as recursive aggregates pose particular challenges. The text also examines the potential shortcomings and complexities of which recursive aggregates are analyzed during the grounding process. The paper is designed to provide a clear and transparent description of how the SAT-based solvers process logic programs, enabling users to identify potential errors or inconsistencies in the algorithms.

A general framework for developing thermodynamics in multi-resource theories has been established. We define a work done by the system as a comprehensive energy change of various resources. This leads to a formulation of the first law of thermodynamics, which is a balance equation for the increase in comprehensive energy and decreases in respective resource levels. We illustrate this with a model of a heat engine that utilizes a mix of electromagnetic and phononic resources to illustrate the output power calculation.

We've developed a new approach to estimating essential information measures, such as mutual information and conditional mutual information, by analyzing the moments of random variables. This approach enabled us to derive several estimators based on the underlying probability distributions. Notably, one of the estimators is a modified version of the classical Radon Nyquist Sampling Theory, which we found to be ill-suited for estimating mutual information in many cases. In contrast, our proposed estimators for information measures are sensitive to changes in the underlying probability distributions and exhibit more consistent performance. Furthermore, this method allows us to identify the key parameters of a conditional probability distribution, specifically the mean and variance, which represent important contributions to the mutual information of two random variables. To validate the effectiveness of our method, we used both artificial and real-world data sets to estimate mutual information in a variety of scenarios, with the results demonstrating the potential advantages of utilizing moment-based estimators over traditional methods.

This research proposes and evaluates an new estimator for identifying common stochastic trends in a multivariate time series using the multivariate vector autoregression model. We examine its asymptotic properties and practical effectiveness by using both simulated data and analyzing the financial SP500 index. Our analysis shows that our estimator is more stable and reliable than existing methods, especially in real-world scenarios characterized by uncertainty and limited data sets.

From a topological perspective, we design quantum codes that operate under unitary transformations without an external metric. Our proposal focuses on a left-right Cayley complex based on the symmetric group's presentations. This results in topological quantum codes capable of efficiently simulating Conway's game of Life. The underlying topology of these codes is closely related to the standard algebraic structure of the group, rather than an external metric. Additionally, we reveal a connection between the Grushko decomposition and the creation of these quantum codes in multiple group representations. Due to the complex nature of the highest-weight states, which serves as the primary source of nonlocal elements in our codes, solving the quantum version of Conway's game is essentially equivalent to solving an NP-hard problem, albeit with a semi-classical approach that takes advantage of the nonlocal properties of the lower-weight states.

The distance-$r$ dominating set problem involves identifying a subset of vertices in a given graph such that every vertex at a distance of $r$ or less is included by at least one selected vertex from the subset. Our research explores the resource limitations of the distance-$r$ dominating set problem in the context of distributed computation on general graphs with multiple vertices. With the parameter $r$ equal to 2, we determine that the constant-time, constant-number of private coins protocols achieving a 1/4 factor approximation or better are inherently probabilistic. Furthermore, we establish that agreeing-on-value protocols with a similar level of performance are disallowed in the setting of Protocols with Bounded Admission. For the more general case where $r$ exceeds 2, we determine that the distance-$r$ dominating set problem remains solvable by simple $O(\log n)$-time protocols in the setting of Adversarial Hands-on Manipulation on basic graph structures like trees. However, we establish the nonexistence of probabilistic protocols achieving a 1/4 factor approximation or better on bipartite graphs with a specific type of sparse structure. On general graphs with a basic label system, we determine that the distance-$r$ dominating set problem allows for solution through a simple $O(\log n)$-time protocols in the setting of Distributed Oracles. We investigate a one-dimensional Dirac Hamiltonian in the presence of both disorder and edge defects. To quantify transport, we employ the Landauer-Büttiker formula, which demonstrates that the bulk mobility gap is not a universal quantity. Rather, it relies on the specific type of edge defect. When the edge defect is semi-transmissive, the bulk mobility gap mimics the edge band gap, but when the edge defect is fully transmissible, the bulk mobility gap coincides with the interband transition gap. A semi-transmissive edge defect is characteristic of higher-order topological insulators, where the bulk mobility gap actually shrinks in response to disorder, unlike the edge band gap which remains unaffected. This phenomenon is analogous to what occurs when the edge defect is fully transmissible. Consequently, we conclude that the bulk mobility gap is not a reliable indicator of the presence of these higher-order topological insulators.

This research investigates the existence of supersymmetry's charginos in search of cases where they decay before they dissociate. To accomplish this, scientists analyzed a 31.3 fb^-1 dataset collected by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider in 2015-2016, operating at 13 TeV. To isolate signals, scientists employed a two-step method: initially, they separated events featuring either three or one large step (hadronically) or one large step (electronically) along with substantial missing energy. Next, scientists used a neural network to distinguish compressed charginos from standard model backgrounds in final events. To identify the compressed mass region, scientists used a shape-based approach on the distribution of second-lepton separation in mass-sensitive events. No evidence beyond the standard model's predicted levels was found. Consequently, scientists derived a lower limit on the chargino mass at 1060 GeV for a mass difference of 0.25 GeV between it and the neutralino, or 930 GeV for a mass difference of 0.05 GeV. Furthermore, scientists extended a previous search for luminous, long-lived charginos in hadronic final states, involving up to 3 electrons/vans, in missing energy and various other factors. To identify the compressed mass region, scientists used a mass-sensitive event distribution in vanishing brane decays. No evidence beyond the standard model's predicted levels was found.
