The Signal app employs PINs to authenticate incoming messages through a more secure method called Signal PINs. Although the mechanism offers enhanced security, users remain unaware of its inner workings, which might impact their behavior. Our study investigates how users comprehend Signal PINs and assesses the effectiveness of a new design principle for creating more secure interactive messages. Through a user study involving 36 participants, we discovered that individuals tend to choose more insecure message PINs when they misunderstand how the authentication mechanism functions. Furthermore, not all users understand the purpose of Signal PINs and some use insecure methods, such as sharing the PIN in plain text. Based on our findings, we propose a new design principle that introduces a more interactive and visible approach to authentication. By implementing an iterative user study with 18 participants, we developed the Design principle for interactive messages, which enhances security by making interactive messages more engaging and visible, reducing the need for user memorization and manual copying of the original message PIN. The new design principle aims to boost security by making interactive messages more engaging and visible, minimizing reliance on user memorization and copying of the original message PIN.

The convergence rate of a new solar-weighted quadrature formula is established and compared with existing ones in the current literature. We assess the accuracy of these quadrature formulas in evaluating the solar integrals function under different scenarios, including when using approximate and tabulated spectral solar irradiance models. Results show that a newly proposed solar-weighted quadrature formula not only exhibits a higher convergence rate but also yields more accurate results in eight out of nine cases compared to existing formulas. Furthermore, this newly proposed quadrature formula is particularly beneficial for applications involving discrete and sporadic data characteristic of solar energy models.

Rapid evaluation of directional derivatives and eigenvalues is a highly demanding requirement in the training of neural networks, accounting for the majority of the time required for each iteration. This paper introduces an efficient algorithm to compute these directional derivatives and eigenvalues with significant speedup, achieving up to a 6-fold improvement. This improved computational cost can be attributed to an innovative strategy of updating only the necessary sub-matrices, rather than the entire structure, following each update of the scale parameter. This novel approach allows for a minimal amount of computation, incur a minimal amount of 'fidelity loss'. To mitigate this loss, we propose a simple adjustment to the ViViT loss term, facilitating a rapid convergence to the optimal orthogonal classifier. This paper showcases the efficacy of the ViViT method in achieving a 1.6-fold improvement in training times while maintaining comparable performance levels on datasets such as Citrus, Citrus-10, and PASCAL-3D+.

We've found that currently available word embeddings, which reflect grammatical gender bias,
exhibit reduced quality when this bias is eliminated. Our focus has been on the impact
of different levels of bias removal compared to a zero bias model. Our experiments
involved generating new word embeddings using a unique method to minimize grammatical
gender bias in Spanish, and two distinct test tasks: text classification using infrequent words
and a zero-shot cross-lingual extraction task. The findings show that our bias-removed embeddings
performed comparably to a model influenced by grammatical gender bias across both tasks,
although the outcomes varied based on the degree of bias removal applied. A thorough evaluation
of the results suggested that our approach successfully eliminated grammatical gender bias
while preserving the desired properties of the embeddings.

For certain groups like finitely generated virtually nilpotent groups, a similar model using affine buildings can be created similar to what is seen in the dynamics of the torus's action on characters. Despite this similarity in structure, there is a distinct difference observed in the dynamics of the action when comparing it to what is seen in the toroidal dynamics, and this is seen to result in the occurrence of an positive lower bound for the number of non-conjugated actions that last for infinite periods. Moreover, different types of elements resulting in different actions when compared can be seen in the dynamics of the action when comparing it to what is seen in the torus's action using characters. Additionally, a simple formula can be seen in the dynamics of the action when comparing it to what is seen in the torus's action using characters that provides the occurrence of the positive lower bound for the number of non-conjugated actions that last for infinite periods.

The problem of estimating the 3D pose of a complex object from a single image has been studied with deep learning-based methods. However, the categories of these objects can be quite broad, like cars or trucks, making it challenging to develop a single effective approach. To tackle this issue, we introduce a novel technique called Multi-Category-PoseNet, a versatile network capable of accurately predicting the pose of various objects within the same image. We achieve this by employing an innovative module that segregates different categories during the training process. Our experiments demonstrate that Multi-Category-PoseNet significantly outperforms our baseline model and existing state-of-the-art approaches, showcasing its superior performance in predicting the pose of multiple objects simultaneously. We also evaluate the efficiency of our method and find that it offers a perfect balance of performance and computational speed. Our code and model will be publicly available at: https://github.com/asharakeh/MC-PoseNet

This paper investigates the capability of graph neural networks to enhance the accuracy of real-time travel time estimation. To gauge GNN performance, we compare it with a state-of-the-art baseline approach utilizing a gradient boosting decision tree model. Our proposal involves a two-part framework where a preliminary stage employs a gradient boosting decision tree model to generate an initial travel time estimate, which is subsequently refined by a GNN-based model. Our empirical evaluation is conducted using the GTD dataset, a real-world dataset derived from GPS data and incorporated into the H4O platform. Our results demonstrate that the hybrid strategy achieves a high R-square value of 83%, significantly outperforming the baseline gradient boosting decision tree model with an R-square value of 75%.

Machine learning's growing influence in high-stakes decision-making has sparked concerns about the fairness of its outputs. Causal inference is cut out for assessing counterfactual fairness in classification problems, as it measures how individual characteristics might affect outcomes using hypothetical "what-if" scenarios. We developed a new Causal Impact Assessment Tool for Evaluation (CHIEF) to evaluate fairness by simulating and comparing minority and majority group members' treatment with different attributes. CHIEF uses a data-driven approach to identify and mitigate confounding factors, ensuring balanced groups for fairness assessment. It consists of an in-depth case study demonstrating CHIEF's ability to evaluate and improve the fairness of a federal loan program's classification process using synthetic data from the US Home Mortgage Disclosure Act. Our results reveal the significance of fairness assessment and highlight CHIEF as a valuable tool for fairness assessment and improvement. CHIEF is now available online as an R package, providing a user-friendly option for fairness assessment and improvement.

Future large-scale radio telescopes, centered on billions of data samples per second, highlight the need for local data processing. The novel, sophisticated HIgh-hardware DEtection instrument on the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope can collect and analyze data in real-time to identify compact sources and schedule follow-up observations online. The instrument's real-time data processing system, enabling fast and flexible analysis of up to 100,000 samples per second from 308 antennas, relies on a distributed computing framework. This is achieved through a combination of CPU and GPU resources for real-time calculations, combined with the use of HEALPix for spherical harmonic transforms and the Root framework for task management. The instrument also features real-time data storage through a combination of floating-point file writing and in-memory caching, enabling data recovery in case of power loss. The instrument's real-time capabilities have been successfully tested with real data, leading to the detection of sources previously overlooked due to their low signal-to-noise ratio. The results of these online observations, encompassing over 1,600 sources in the galaxy Centaurus A, are made available through a publicly accessible repository.

Metaphotonics incorporates light and matter through a single interaction, employing optical inducements of electric and magnetic resonances in matter. Research in this field largely relies on structuring non-magnetic (dielectric) materials that leverage unit cells with non-resonant, negatively refracting properties to manipulate photons. Our work presents an alternative approach involving dielectric structures comprised of metallic balls for metaphotonics applications. We demonstrated that these configurations can generate unique anti-resonant phenomena, which enable the realization of metaphotonically-designed diffraction patterns, dispersion relations, and negative refraction at a macroscopic scale. Notably, the anti-resonant patterns within these systems exhibit resilience to variations in size and shape of the constitutive elements. This study provides fundamental insights for metaphotonics applications and serves as a benchmark for physical-optics research, complementing existing schemes based on resonant phenomena.

The box office performance of a movie can be influenced by many factors,
including the popularity of its leading actors, the effectiveness of its direction,
and various other attributes that contribute to a film's overall quality. In this study,
we employed a collaborative filtering approach to analyze the correlation between
movie attributes and revenue. A novel metric was developed to measure an actor's
influence on a film's success, and when adjusted for varying performance levels,
the result revealed that a actor's impact remains relatively consistent across different
films. Additionally, we found that revenue can be accurately predicted using a list of
movie attributes including, but not limited to, budget, runtime, and the number of
nominations received. Ultimately, this analysis identified several key attributes that
affect a movie's success and provided a predictive model that could prove valuable to
both investors and directors in making more informed decisions.

This paper presents a new model of the European electric grid network for studying small signal stability and frequency fluctuations. It analyzes the secondary frequency regulation system and proves a key stability property using the Gramian method. Based on this finding, the author creates a quadratic optimization problem to design secondary frequency control strategies that enhance small signal stability, focusing on damping certain transfer function poles. Simulation results indicate that the proposed control strategies offer improved stability and faster damping of certain network dynamics while ensuring secure power exchange between nodes. Moreover, the design parameters allow for a trade-off between stability and costs associated with control actions.

This research focuses on developing a control framework for adaptive distributed optimization of complex cyber-physical systems with interconnected structures. Two key levels of its architectural framework are the control level and the infrastructure level. At the control level, a collaborative control system allows multiple cyber-physical agents to automatically adjust their control strategies in response to changing system conditions without needing prior knowledge of the environment. At the infrastructure level, a network of nodes disseminates dynamic systems information to the agents. This paper introduces a comprehensive framework for adaptive distributed optimization of complex cyber-physical systems, leveraging both the control and infrastructure layers to facilitate learning within the agents. The convergence of the optimization algorithm is formally demonstrated, and we verify the effectiveness of the proposed framework through numerical experiments.

Future missions aimed at studying the polarization of UV/X-ray emissions from remote blazars may uncover detailed information about their surrounding astrophysical environment. By analyzing the degree and angle of polarization across various wavelengths, researchers can investigate the complex behavior of these objects' jet streams and the impact of different processes on their emission patterns. A novel technique utilizes the relationship between polarization angle and distance to infer the position and characteristics of interstellar scattering sites, one of which could lie as far as 100 parsecs away. Our analysis suggests that a reliable determination of the degree and angle of polarization, with an accuracy of about 1% and 1 degree respectively, is required for a detection to be confirmed. Given the polarization measurements will be close to the instrument's capacity to detect, a comprehensive approach will be needed to trust any findings.

We explore the analytical characteristics of the Hessian matrices derived from imaginary-time path integrals in two categories of systems: those with one-step replica-symmetry-breaking and those with many-step replica-symmetry-breaking. Notably, systems with one-step RSB, such as the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model, exhibit uniformly positive or semi-definite Hessian matrices, whereas those with many-step RSB, such as the random energy model, feature negative diagonal entries and non-symmetric off-diagonal vectors in the Hessian. We establish the mathematical foundation for these distinctions by developing an algorithm for computing the Hessian, validating its convergence and analytical properties through the context of the random energy model and its one-step and many-step RSB counterparts.

This study investigates the limitations of ideal quantum cloners in protecting systems 
from being cloned in asymptotically optimal conditions. It compares the performance 
of two key online schemes: one proposed by Bia\l{y} et al. in PRL 97, 200501 (2006) 
that ensures coherence and the recently introduced all-noise scheme by Buisson et al. 
in PRL 123, 150402 (2019) that disqualifies itself by always cloning incorrectly. 
The work assesses the schemes' efficiency in cloning three symmetric states with 
constant overlap and a mixture of Gaussian states, also examining the trade-off 
between efficiency and correctness. It reveals that the all-noise scheme consistently 
performs at or near optimal levels in most cases, often surpassing the ideal 
cloner's achievements. The analysis further explores a hybrid scheme, designed to 
identify a specific subset of qubit states, and demonstrates its potential as a 
practical, constant-error solution for a wide range of cloning tasks.

We have developed a mass-density model for light baryons based on the mass patterns of light mesons in QCD. This approach starts with the N/N interquark coupling potential from the N-N potential derived by the resonating group method, combining it with a linear QCD confinement confine potential and a simple N/QCD quasibaryon function. By using this framework, we have revised our earlier work on the N, N*, and Lambda series in 3D, and have obtained a mass spectrum that aligns with experimental masses for the N and N* states, and a mass spectrum with reasonable agreement for the Lambda series. This model also enables the calculation of the residual mass of the N, N*, and Lambda states. We have also used this revised model to study the Delta series. In addition, we have explored the N, N*, and Lambda mass matrices in 3D for both the N-N and N/omega transition potentials. These investigations have significant implications for studying the N-N interaction and the decuplet-baryon spectrum in QCD.

The Sun's underlying meridional circulation is crucial for understanding the geometric structure and dynamic processes of the solar interior and atmosphere. Acoustic waves, detected through sunspot observations, can travel long distances and may reveal crucial information about the circulation pattern. By analyzing acoustic wave travel times, we hope to better grasp the geometry of the sun's circulation system. However, the non-linear nature of sunspots makes it challenging to interpret the acoustic waves without a deep understanding of the surrounding mechanical waves. In this research, we explore how mechanical waves, recorded during a sunspot observation on October 15, 2017, can affect the appearance of acoustic waves and how these waves might appear in numerical simulations. By superimposing the simulated and observed acoustic waves, we are able to accurately reconstruct the sun's circulation pattern at the depths of 55 Mm below the solar surface.

The existence of a primordial magnetic field is a possibility that has increased due to its observed relationships with the number density and temperature fluctuations. We investigated how such a magnetic field might affect the propagation of gravitational waves produced during inflation, using mathematical formulas to consider varying levels of magnetization. We found that the gravitational waves could remain closely aligned in the same direction, with certain orientations remaining perpendicular to the magnetic field. Additionally, we found that the perpendicular alignment has a higher probability and magnitude in the magnetic field effects. What's more, the magnetic field may impact the detection of the gravitational waves, potentially lowering the required sensitivity of the experiment to detect the waves. The magnetic field could also make the detection more feasible with a lower experimental sensitivity. Consequently, the magnetic field may both hinder and facilitate the detection of the gravitational waves.

We propose a disparity-aided model to enhance the compression of 4D light field images by leveraging additional depth information. The suggested approach entails encoding light field and depth data separately and incorporating depth predictions into a light field compression model. This increased reliance on depth data enables the light field compression model to be fine-tuned and improved. Furthermore, to facilitate rapid encoding and decoding processes, we incorporate circular buffer (CB) techniques into our light field compression scheme. The proposed CB-LS model outperforms existing standards in terms of PSNR and MS-SSIM, achieving a notable improvement of +2.80, +2.25, +2.35, and +2.21 dB, +0.044, +0.058, +0.060, and +0.041 SSIM, respectively, at similar bitrates.

This study presents a groundbreaking approach to achieving cross-lingual information retrieval (CLR) through a novel, semi-interactive mechanism. The approach dubbed semi-interactive CLR, enhances the accuracy of retrieval processes by minimizing overspecification and accommodating user input in a flexible manner. A seamless extension of previous CLR models, our approach achieves the same results while offering more flexibility and accuracy. A collaborative experiment with both researchers and real users reveals its advantages and efficiency in user studies. A supplementary user study demonstrates the practicality and user satisfaction derived from our method, semi-interactive CLR.

Spatial models with precise details are required to analyze demographic data with similar details. A novel continuous-space model (MCSP) for studying animal populations has been developed, combining a spatial point process model for species presence with a density estimation model for abundance. This demographic model has been implemented using a Bayesian approach based on Gaussian processes (GP) and related techniques. A non-parametric estimation method for the abundance surface GP has been devised to address issues related to estimating abundance surfaces. This method has been evaluated through simulations and is then employed to analyze data from the study on the spatial distribution of a European population of the island fox (Urocyon py. pygmeus).

By treating the quantum memory model as a comprehensive multi-step gambling system, this study identifies a strategy that yields the highest possible outcomes. This finding introduces the quantum memory model into a broader range of gambling systems, and a novel analytical approach is applied to a classic problem. To determine the optimal betting pattern, a detailed analysis of the quantum memory model is conducted, and a fundamental equation for the gambler's expected return is established. A key discovery in this context involves the identification of a function that decreases rapidly, which set the stage for a central limit theorem application. Utilizing this novel function, a precise calculation of the gambler's expected return is achieved, and it reveals that the return approaches a normal distribution as the number of steps increases. Moreover, the optimal betting pattern is pinpointed, and our results are corroborated by numerical simulations.

A search for the decay $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ has been carried out using 2016 proton-proton collision data at a 13 TeV center-of-mass energy collected by the LHCb detector. The data set a new upper limit of $3\times 10^{-9}$ for the branching ratio of $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ and a new, more precise upper limit of $6\times 10^{-10}$ after applying a cut that removes any resonance structure associated with the decay.

Simulating the development of turbulence in a model disk at various stages of its formation can help researchers understand how planet formation occurs within the disk. Utilizing an updated version of the BEEBE code, which incorporates the effects of magnetic fields in a more realistic manner, we have obtained a range of disk models that exhibit distinct levels of turbulence. These models are based on two different idealized scenarios: one representing the central inner region of the disk and another depicting the outer disk at a later time. In the first scenario, we note that the disk's mid-plane is relatively calm, with low levels of turbulence, whereas the upper layers exhibit heightened activity. In contrast, the later-time model, which is characteristic of the disk's main mass accumulation phase, shows uniform turbulence throughout the disk, with no distinction between the mid-plane and the upper layers. Our results suggest that the disk's turbulence state can be used to determine its age and the time at which the disk's magnetic field gives way to the viscous dissipation that facilitates the development of protoplanets.

To determine the optimal arrangement of antennas in an autocorrelation phase difference system for atmospheric distortion compensation, we're exploring various antenna configurations. Our research involves assessing the performance of atmospheric models (AMDs) in maximizing signal strength. We've found that some atmospheric models, such as the Tuck, series E, and series D models, excel in the blue end of the spectrum but fall short in the red end. On the other hand, the series C model performs well in the red end but poorly in the blue end. After analyzing the effective number of parameters for each model, we recommend the Tuck series D model due to its simplicity and effectiveness for ADC designs.

This study aims to enhance direct simulation Monte Carlo methods for high-dimensional models by leveraging a Bayesian neural network with a non-convex prior. Initially, the Bayesian neural network is trained on a high-dimensional model using data from a rough estimate, and the input variables are modeled more effectively. Consequently, the indirect Monte Carlo approach yields significantly better results compared to the direct method, particularly for large spaces to explore. Notably, the indirect approach using the Bayesian neural network surpasses the statistical efficiency of the direct approach by at least one order of magnitude.

Our approach involves establishing a correspondence between local type spaces in continuous logic and certain compact topological spaces. We then demonstrate that these type spaces can be linked with a duality phenomenon observed in abelian groups. Based on this understanding, a notion of 'tame' logic is proposed, with the associated type spaces serving as key components. Furthermore, a concept of 'tame' abelian group is introduced in relation to this approach.

The machine learning industry is now addressing ethics as a vital consideration.
Satisfying users' privacy requirements involves balancing privacy and utility.
Differential privacy offers a recognized framework for ensuring privacy in the machine learning pipeline, while federated learning enables parallel training on devices. To promote fairness, metrics such as fairness metrics are employed to inform algorithm design. As the industry grows, there is an increasing need for comprehensive ethics machine learning model development tools. To address this need, we introduce the Open Federated Learning (OFL) framework, which incorporates differential privacy and fairness metrics to support ethics machine learning. The OFL framework includes a planning tool for learning pipeline development, a validator for checking fairness and privacy constraints, and a commander for executing and managing OFL applications. The OFL framework is now available for public use on GitHub.

In a feebly interacting dark sector model involving a U(1)' extension of the standard model, the introduction of a dark matter-like particle, specifically a sterile neutrino with a non-zero mass, results in a substantial dark matter relic abundance. Furthermore, the proposed model enables the production of a $Z^{\prime}$ boson at particle colliders like the LHC, which in turn decays into the dark matter-like particle and a dark photon. We have investigated the associated implications for dark matter searches and the design of future neutrino experiments, specifically the Deep Underground Neutrino Detector (DUNE) in the context of its current design specifications. The results of our analysis reveal the potential for DUNE to either restrict or detect the $Z^{\prime}$ boson, depending on its mass and coupling strength, offering a competitive alternative to current particle colliders. The findings of our analysis further suggest the necessity for further optimization in the detector design of future experiments in order to improve their capabilities for dark matter searches at neutrino experiments.

The growing interest in deep unsupervised learning (DSL) models stems from their potential to enhance various wireless communication systems, particularly channel state information (CSI) estimation, where current algorithms face performance limitations due to their relative immaturity. To address this, a novel approach utilizing a $n$-order manifold structure in CSI measurements is presented, aiming to bypass the need for direct parameter training and parameter collection. By leveraging existing genetic algorithms as a priori model, this method achieves functional CSI measurement classification and achieves state estimation. Performance comparisons using real-world data from 86 wireless networks demonstrate a significant 60% relative improvement in estimation accuracy for the $n$=8 structure over traditional genetic algorithms, alongside a notable 94% reduction in computational requirements.

Our research demonstrates that $\beta$-strenght functions derived from the superfluid nuclear matrix element method ($\beta$SF-NME) exhibit significant variations based on the specific nuclear configurations of both the parent and daughter nuclei in decay transitions. The impacts of the nuclear wave functions' collective and paired configurations on these functions are thoroughly analyzed. Notably, our study reveals that the accuracy of $\beta$SF-NME relies heavily on its ability to correctly account for the parent and daughter nucleus wave functions' similarities. Furthermore, we observed that adjustments in the nuclear matrix elements' energy normalization could help rectify the differences between these functions and the experimental Q$_{\beta}$-values. The influence of quasiparticle effects, particle-hole excitations, and pairing energies on the $\beta$SF-NME is also discussed in relation to its dependence on the nuclear deformation.

This discussion centers around a dark sector model featuring two left-handed fermions and a scalar field that exists in its singlet state. The left-handed fermions autonomously acquire mass through the Higgs mechanism, while the singlet scalar field generates a non-zero VEV within the dark sector. This leads to a mass determination for a dark matter candidate, one option being a fermion that is both Majorana and scalar coupled due to the presence of the singlet scalar. Furthermore, a mechanism exists by which this dark matter candidate decays to a right-handed neutrino and a scalar particle, leading to a mass range for the dark matter candidate that is consistent with observed relic densities.

We introduce an algorithm that uses learning-based control to optimize the performance of closed-loop system regulators, utilizing data generated by a model-based system predictor to guide controller updates. A data-efficient learning strategy is developed that leverages the predictive model's capabilities to identify system dynamics and efficiently train controllers for optimal performance. Our approach is tested against conventional reinforcement learning methods and the performance benefits are validated through comprehensive experiments with various dynamic systems and diverse performance objectives in different environments.

We've derived spin-three Ward identities for four-point correlation functions in a specific type of Toda field theory. The analysis shows that these identities align with the principles of higher-spin symmetry. Building upon this, we have developed a systematic approach for describing a specific set of Ward identities among the four-point functions. The identities are characterized by specific combinations of higher-spin operators that maintain their structure across the various choices of chemical potentials within the Toda theory. The analysis also sheds light on the connection between the particle-like operators in the free field limit and the higher-spin operators. The paper further discusses how the derived spin operators adhere to a set of principles involving their mutual commutation, a key aspect in achieving the free field limit. The analysis provided serves as a foundation for exploring the free field limit in the context of one-dimensional higher-spin conformal field theories.

Within the realm of Generative Adversarial Networks, relation embeddings have been proposed as a means to enhance the ability of GANs to generate images relevant to given prompts. This goal is acheived by incorporating a prompt conditioning technique that enables the generator to incorporate relation embeddings into its architecture. The prompt is passed through a relation network, allowing it to capture intricate connections between words and images, and the relation embedding is subsequently sent to the generator. Theoretical analyses reveal that previous relation embeddings lacked the capability to guide the generator in creating images and, as a result, underutilized their potential. The proposed relation embeddings, on the other hand, serve as optimal discriminators, facilitating higher image generation quality with greater sincerity. Experimental findings demonstrate that relation embeddings optimized with PCE lead to significantly improved image generation tasks, and notable gains can be attained by incorporating just a few well-optimized relation embeddings.

A new approach for achieving global phase control in twin-field quantum key distribution (TFQKD) using partial swapping of entangled photons between two nodes has been developed. By employing a reference frame to determine time differences between light travel times in the horizontal and vertical directions, the proposed scheme successfully avoids the necessity for precise measurement timing in the main experiments. As a result, the complexity of the experiment is reduced and global phase locking can be efficiently achieved through the use of the reference frame, which also helps to eliminate potential phase errors. Several global phase locks have been achieved with different time delays and reported in this work. Additionally, the feasibility of the reference frame method is further validated by demonstrating a TFQKD entanglement verification without precise timing, which is an essential capability for achieving global phase control.

This paper examines connections between Toeplitz operators acting on p-Bergman and p-Fock spaces and a specific algebra generated by a set of polynomials within these spaces. It builds upon a prior study by the authors and extends the findings to the setting of bounded symbols across the unit ball in multi-dimensional space. In this expanded context, the relationships between Weyl transforms, Toeplitz operators, and the algebra of polynomials are established, generalized from a previous publication by the authors, which focused on the case of unbounded symbols in the one-dimensional setting.

Recently, pseudo labeling techniques have contributed significantly to the advancement of object detection. This approach involves using an object detector to generate annotations for a training set, with the goal of improving performance on a reference set, often differing in quality or quantity. However, due to the inherent challenges of object detection, earlier methods' results were not consistently better than that of the original annotations. In order to address these limitations, we propose an efficient method for obtaining highly accurate pseudo annotations. In an attempt to bridge the gap between detection results and bounding-box accuracy, we introduce a cross-ensemble approach by combining the detection model with a bounding-box transformer, utilizing attention-based features and transformer encoding to enhance representation quality. A novel propagation strategy is also developed to preserve the integrity of label data during the pseudo labeling process. In comprehensive evaluations on the Pascal VOC and COCO datasets, our approach is shown to produce significantly better pseudo annotations, resulting in a notable performance boost in comparison to state-of-the-art methods.

Our research focuses on determining the spatial distribution of hydrogen, helium, and other elements within NGC2024's Veil nebula through spectral analysis and wide-field observations made possible by large-scale instruments such as VLT-GLACIAR, Chandra, and XMM-Newton. By examining Veil nebula's gas and dust, we gain insight into the star formation process that initiated this phenomenon and the subsequent interactions between it and ultraviolet radiation. Velocities of gas within the Veil nebula, identified as HII regions HII-A and HII-B along with an HII streamer, reveal complex multi-component systems. HII-A's and HII-B's velocities match the values of B stars within the region, while HII-B's velocities are influenced by the cloud's motion. HII-A's and HII-B's emission is weakened by self-absorption signals from neutral gas, detectable in radio and X-ray wavelengths, near the Veil nebula's edge and within HII-B towards the cloud's center. HII-B's and HII streamer's spectra show a helium to hydrogen ratio close to the cosmic value, but this ratio for HII-A is lower than both the cosmic and HII-B values. HII-A's and HII-B's ionic temperatures vary from 1.0 to 1.4 10^4 K, while the cosmic and HII-B temperatures range between 1.0 10^4

Transformers have been favorably compared to convolutional networks due to their improved translation out-of-vocabulary words and enhanced generalizability. However, it remains to be determined if this performance comes at the expense of speed. If so, the choice between these models would rest on a trade-off between processing speed and computational efficiency. Our research suggests that this is indeed the case. We discovered that the processing speeds of Transformers and convolutional networks with comparable task performance are in fact interchangeable. Both classes of models can be modified to yield the other's characteristics using depth-wise convolution and splitting operations, which come with a minimal reduction in performance. We further refine these operations to eliminate residual connections from the architectures, leading to a new understanding of the relationship between Layers(N, F) in Transformers and a new interpretation of the Scale-Ambiguity problem in terms of operation-mixing rather than feature-mixing.

The primary objective is to forecast future mortality rates rather than evaluating insurance value, despite classic models being effective in doing so. We propose a innovative approach based on Markov chain factors that outperforms traditional methods by leveraging time-varying factor loadings. To maintain the univariate distribution and calculate predictive probabilities, we'll establish a resampling technique similar to Diebold and Mariano's 2002 framework. To evaluate our model's performance over time, we'll utilize the Mean Absolute Error metric. Extensive analysis will be conducted using the $\text{PP2015}$ dataset to refine the resampling procedure and optimize the model. Furthermore, we'll investigate the impact of different priors and their influence on the forecast quality.

The rapidly evolving field of neural architecture search (NAS) is driven by its limitless potential for improving, yet current top-tier results are achieved not by optimizing architectures but by leveraging highly advanced language models like RoBERTa and ELECTRA to generate superior results. Although these models exhibit high performance in many tasks, significantly reducing their size through pruning yields unexpected outcomes such as diminished ability to recognize out-of-distribution data and lower prediction accuracy. To counter this, we develop a pioneering technique for automatically reinitializing the weights of these models according to a predefined structure, thereby revitalizing their core characteristics and restoring their high-performance standards. Building on this foundation, we developed an innovative NAS approach based on a refined variant of the ReZero NAS architecture that significantly outperforms all previous NAS models without resorting to expensive search processes, thereby serving as a strong foundation for future NAS advancements.

Time-series data are prominent in research and industry due to their widespread presence across various domains. Their analysis necessitates a direct representation of time series, which is often referred to as a time-series feature. Extracting an optimal set of features from time series has become a vital concern in time-series analysis. Despite a few leading packages, the community still faces several limitations in time-series feature extraction. The primary issue is the lack of a unified platform that addresses the diverse requirements of time-series feature extraction. The proposed package, theft, seeks to address this limitation by providing an extensive collection of time-series features through a simple and flexible framework based on R6 classes. The package also enables the creation of custom features and features with distinct encodings. Additionally, it supports the integration of existing time-series packages such as tseries, gybms, and WeatherData. The package includes a decorator-style API for efficient and dynamic computation of features. It also facilitates the data transformation of popular time-series datasets and popular deep learning-based architectures for time-series analysis.
We demonstrate that in a complete CAT(0) space, geodesic completeness is equivalent to the condition that the fundamental group is freely generated as an amalgamated free product.

A key aspect of translating content into another language involves both translating and reviewing the work to ensure its quality, though this process is often understudied. Despite several systems and tools being developed for translation quality assessment, there is a lack of comprehensive research on how to effectively evaluate the performance of both translators and reviewers. In our research, we have established a new evaluation approach that analyzes translation and review simultaneously, rather than separately, which allows us to compare both translators and reviewers in a single assessment. We have also developed a review quality assessment tool that employs a set of explicit evaluation criteria, along with corresponding features, to evaluate review quality. We have applied this tool to evaluate both the translation and review performance of over 400 translators and reviewers who worked on a dataset of NASA technical documents, and have identified several key insights. These insights have significant practical implications and can be used in both translation and review post-editing projects. We have also conducted a more in-depth examination of the performance of individual reviewers, similar to how translator performance is often evaluated, in order to identify their strengths and weaknesses.

The concept of eigenchannels has been applied in various fields, such as wave and transport theory. The introduction of waves into a many-channel system induces a natural separation into eigenchannels corresponding to the spatial intensity distributions within the system. We have found an analytical solution for the eigenfunctions of a linear coupled wave equation with a complex coefficient in a periodic potential. The eigenfunctions possess a natural separation into two groups: where the intensity distribution matches the eigenchannel concept and behaves as a spatial mode at the system's output. We have derived an analytical expression for the eigenvalues using the Fourier method and been able to compensate for the error in existing works using this approach. Additionally, we have determined the relationship between coupling strength and wave phase shift. Finally, we have obtained a general expression for the eigenfunctions using a special type of limit.

We examine the effect of iterative magnitude pruning on the accuracy and speed of neural networks to bridge the gap between theoretical benefits and practical outcomes. By adjusting the 'keep rate' iteratively, we assess the performance and memory usage of pruned networks at various stages. Our experiments using QuantVGG6 on CIFAR10/VRT show that iterative magnitude pruning achieves a 1.9% higher top-1 accuracy compared to a one-shot method, while also reducing parameters by 85.8% and the storage requirement to 94.2%. Conversely, when using CIFAR100/VRT with Random Quantization, we observe an 8.2% accuracy drop at each iteration, indicating that pruning is less effective when the datasets and quantization are less compatible. Our analysis of training dynamics suggests that current iterative algorithms may be biased towards inclusion, leading to inaccurate accuracy predictions and over-pruning. Therefore, we suggest a more reliable approach involving multiple criteria.

The growing adoption of blockchain technology in the gaming sector has led to the emergence of blockchain-based lotteries, which are now played by a rising number of users. Yet, there has been a lack of in-depth analysis into the interaction between users and lottery operators in this area. In this study, a blockchain-based lottery platform called 'Lottery' was designed and the results obtained after performing 79,852 rounds of experimentation are presented. The findings show that the current blockchain-based lottery infrastructure is prone to exploitation by users who can win big, resulting in negative returns for the majority of users. By employing 'fake transaction flooding', a new attack technique was detected that can be used by users to manipulate the lottery outcome at a rate of $O(\sqrt{n}/m)$, where $n$ represents the round number and $m$ is the block size of the blockchain, leading to a $O(n^{3/8})$ time complexity. The observed outcomes demonstrate that the jackpot range of 94% to 100% is required to provide a positive return to users, and the return on investment for users is consistently negative when the jackpot is less than 91%. Furthermore, the user base is found to be in a state of 'free rider's dilemma' and the lottery operators generate revenue solely through block fees, highlighting the need for an alternative business model that rewards users for their participation.

By carefully analyzing the critical behavior of a lattice Yang-Mills theory at a specific Renormalization Group fixed point known as the Yang-Mills fixed point (YMF), we investigate how the number of charge states impacts the critical properties of this system. A large-charge expansion is employed to determine various critical exponents of the YMF, which are then compared against Monte Carlo simulations and theoretical predictions from a different method. While the derived exponent ratios match the simulated results quite well, our large-charge expansion results in slightly higher values for the anomalous dimension and critical exponent $\nu$, with approximately 3% and 15% discrepancies, respectively. The large-charge expansion appears to yield accurate results at charge states far beyond what's achievable in Monte Carlo simulations, providing a useful theoretical framework.

The presence of a nonuniform strain field in a two-dimensional Dirac valley model leads to transport mechanisms other than quantum Hall effects. A strain field that varies sinusoidally across the sample gives rise to valley-dependent twist angles, mimicking the effects of a Berry phase. By analyzing the conductivity tensor, researchers have found that this geometry confers the quantum Hall phenomenon not only in the plane but also in higher-dimensional spaces, known as the hyper-Schwinger model. A specific investigation of a finite, twisted toroidal sample reveals how its geometry and parameters, such as period and electron density, interplay to produce distinct quantum Hall behaviors.

Active learning techniques like Model Soup can enhance the generalization capabilities of adaptive models. We show that its performance is comparable to other strategies such as Double Domain Domain Adaptive Learning Assumption, and its strength lies in its ability to reuse knowledge from other tasks when faced with new domains that have similar distribution to existing tasks. We also discovered that using SOUP's knowledge transfer method leads to a positive correlation between domain similarity and performance. Building upon this, we created a method called Domain Soup, to address the challenge of making predictions on multiple target domains with different characteristics. Using a combination of learned knowledge and domain-specific data from other targets, we demonstrated that Domain Soup yields better performance than simply using additional target data. We highlight the potential of using multiple targets to improve model performance, and suggest future research directions in this area.

t-SNE is a highly regarded visualization technique although its integration into large-scale data sets has been hindered by its computational intensity. A key element in t-SNE is modeling proximity between non-close data points using a Gaussian distribution. This approach leads to a simplified, yet approximate method for modeling neighbor distributions based on the nearest neighbors, which is suitable for the algorithm. However, this basic approach may not be necessary as it turns out the proximal distributions of spherical distributions are better represented by a Dirichlet distribution than the Gaussian. As a result, we've created a variant of t-SNE that uses the Dirichlet distribution for modeling neighbor distributions, which we call d-t-SNE. By doing so, we've been able to show that our approach not only provides a more accurate approximation than the traditional method but also allows for a more efficient computation. In our experiments, we've found that the traditional t-SNE and our d-t-SNE have comparable performance, however we've been able to achieve significant time optimizations by using optimized methods for a few critical components and a more efficient method for modeling neighbor distributions. Furthermore, we've been able to achieve an even better approximation of the true neighbor distribution by integrating a supervised projection step in the learning process of d-t-SNE. This new algorithm is called s-d-t-SNE and it offers not only an improved approximation of the true neighbor distribution but also allows for a more precise integration of labels in the learning process, resulting in a more accurate

The polaron wave function is heavily influenced by the level of electron interaction, and when interaction is weak, a particular wave function approach works well. However, when interaction is strong, a different wave function approach is more accurate. In studying the wave function approach that works well in weak interactions, we've found a full series of diagrams in two dimensions that describe how energy changes in a system. We've found a relation in this series that helps us understand how energy changes, and we've used this to figure out the tendency of a system to change its energy when it interacts with a particular force. We've compared our result to a simpler, well-established way of understanding this tendency and found it's mostly accurate, except for very strong interactions. We've also seen that at very strong interactions, a different simple, well-established way of understanding this tendency gives a better result. Additionally, we've investigated how the level of electron interaction affects the tendency of a system to change its energy and how this affects the behavior of a particular type of particle.

In fermionic systems, the application of digital-analog quantum computing to the Fermi-Hubbard model has been made possible through the utilization of transmon qubits paired with micromagnets. This approach enables the tuning of the transmon-qubit spectrum by placing it within a variable magnetic field, thus creating a non-Abelian gauge flux that results in an effective Hilbert space confined to a finite fermionic subspace. We have developed a hybrid quantum-logic operation to simulate the Fermi-Hubbard model, allowing for the efficient calculation of the model's parameters using a poly-factorization circuit of minimal depth. We have demonstrated that this approach provides a quantum advantage by achieving a similar fidelity relative to a classical Monte Carlo calculation of the model's parameters at a significantly reduced cost. Additionally, the inhomogeneity of the magnetic field has been found to have a minimal impact on the performance of the simulator. We have shown that the hybrid quantum-logic approach has the capacity to efficiently solve problems related to the model's parameters and the long-term dynamics of the model. Moreover, the model itself can be viewed as a specific realization of a digital-analog quantum computer's quantum dynamics.

The study of matching polynomials of graphs has been expanded in this paper by examining their duals as a means to analyze the original graphs. In it, we establish the definitions, assess properties and investigate methods to obtain eigenvalue information from them. Additionally, we prove that in the context of specific types of graphs, their matching polynomials exhibit duals that are recognizable as complete, complete bipartite, or complete bipartite with hyperedges of size 2, 3, or a combination of these.

We categorize a set of quantum representations of the genus 2 mapping class group that are minimal in a specific sense, mirroring Dehn's representations in the context of hyperbolicity. We demonstrate that these representations are unique up to trivial equivalences and leverage the simplicial structure of the complex of curves to establish this uniqueness, showcasing a blend of geometric and harmonic analysis principles. We further calculate the unitary orbits of these representations, given the mapping class group's unitary nature, and exploit the representations' invariance under the Jacobi group to obtain a compact description of these orbits. We conclude by providing a precise formula for the number of elements in each orbit.

In 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic prompted a sudden shift to remote work arrangements, forcing organizations and projects to adapt. Prior to this global crisis, many initiatives had already begun embracing Scrum methodologies to enhance their flexibility and responsiveness. Our study aims to determine the relationship between Scrum implementation and project success in the context of remote work. We conducted a cross-sectional survey among 292 projects and analyzed the data using structural equation modeling and permutation testing. Our results show that Scrum's impact on project success in remote work settings is modest and only significant in cases where teams are partially distributed.

This paper verifies the classification of all arrowhead matrices up to a specified size, and it also explores their linear transformations and various characteristics. Notably, the study reveals that the Gau--Wu number for these matrices does not serve as a distinct characteristic when their entries are freely variable.

A study estimating the interplay between CPT violation and long-distance charm and beauty decays has been conducted using a data set of $6.46$ of $pp$ collisions, collected at the LHCb experiment at an energy of $13~\text{TeV}$. A selection of hadrons containing a muon, which result from the decays of $D$, $D^*$, $B$, and $K$ particles, is made through identifying the muon's partner and the particle's momentum. These hadrons are categorized based on their displacement from the original interaction point in the $z$-direction and their momenta. A fit to this distribution, which includes models of particle movement in the $z$-hypothesis, reveals that beauty particles' average proper decay length is significantly lower compared to charm particles and other background sources. A fit also yields an estimate for CPT-violating asymmetry, which is found to be less than three orders in magnitude smaller than the known limit. A corresponding fit to the particle distribution along the $z$-axis in events containing two muons reveals that an asymmetry exists and that it is in line with the standard model predictions.

This research explores the application of topological methods in analyzing politics by examining the racial segregation of school districts in St. Louis, Missouri. We utilize persistent homology to analyze how racial groups interact within a topological space and evolve over time. By applying this approach, we can capture both subtle and dramatic changes in racial segregation over time. By applying the techniques of persistent homology, we can create a topological model of racial segregation in the metropolitan area of St. Louis, revealing dynamic changes in racial separation and identifying 'wells' or regions where racial interaction is more intense. We compare our approach to the well-known measures of segregation such as the Index of Segregation and the Isolation Index, showing that these metrics often fail to capture the dynamic and complex patterns of racial separation observed in our topological model.

In massive machine-type communication scenarios involving a vast number of users making intermittent, infrequent transmissions into a shared channel, we examine the interplay between two neighboring stations' power management strategies. Specifically, we assess the efficacy of binary power control (BPC) in comparison to optimal power control (OPC) when both are governed by the long-term power utilization rules. To this end, we recast the power control problem as a channel allocation issue in a weighted bipartite graph, reducing it to a randomized rounding of a dual feasible solution obtained via Lagrangian dualization. This approach yields an analysis that shows BPC achieves a constant factor of the optimal power control, approximately, under certain conditions. Moreover, via the generated power allocation matrices, we derive concise, explicit expressions for the average received signal-to-noise ratios of both receivers. Finally, a consideration of the intertemporal aspects of the issue is taken when generalizing these results to settings where received signal strengths are subject to constraints.

A crucial component of financial audits involves verifying management's claims about the financial statements. Recent studies in this area primarily focused on detecting deception in isolated statements, whereas real-world audits involve numerous claims made by one person. To address this, a new approach using natural language processing, a mathematical framework for uncertainty, and a model of lying has been developed that takes into account a auditor's lack of knowledge. Unlike previous methods, this one does not assume a single true statement must be hidden among false ones. Instead, it allows for a blend of accurate and inaccurate statements, represented through Dempster-Shafer mass functions that capture a auditor's uncertainties. A novel learning algorithm is presented that can be trained without a supervisor, relying on a game-like interaction with a auditor. A comprehensive evaluation revealed that this method significantly outperforms other approaches in this area, particularly when handling complex, natural language inputs.

A new approach called Acceptance Rejection Stitching, first developed for simulating Poisson processes, has the ability to generalise to any type of point process. This is based on the point process's radon density, which represents the density of the process's marks as it relates to the underlying space. The technique creates a rejection sampling process that efficiently simulates the point process while maintaining independence from the underlying space. A practical guide on implementing Acceptance Rejection Stitching for common point processes is provided and its advantages over existing simulation methods are discussed. This simulation technique is particularly valuable for estimating features in natural images, a task where typical point processes may not adequately simulate an image's properties.

The Galilean transformations are revised in line with the Generalized Uncertainty Principle's deformed algebra.  The associated quantum field algebra generates a set of first-order differential operators that adapt classical velocity measurements, leading to a distinct set of differential equations.  By using a streamlined approach, this revised Searle's group is characterized and shown to be a nonPoincaré, nonAbelian Lie group named the deformed Galilean group.  Its corresponding deformed Galilean algebra distinguishes itself from its standard counterpart.  The deformed Galilean group's structure is such that it includes a nonAbelian nilpotent Lie algebra with a nilpotent core and a nonnilpotent Abelian Lie algebra with a nilpotent quotient, yielding various diverse and significant applications.

This letter presents a novel multi-stage multi-band (MSMB) scheduling approach, which efficiently utilizes resources in a complex multitasking environment. A centralized algorithm is developed to create a multi-stage schedule that accounts for the dynamic transfer of tasks between stages. A theoretical analysis demonstrates that in a central processor, the existing multi-band scheduling (MS) principle can be applied to schedule tasks with different sharing ratios of processing capacity. Notably, varying this ratio leads to distinct scheduling patterns. A simulated environment is used to validate the proposed scheduling approach and demonstrate its feasibility in a multi-stage setting.

Robots requiring powerful feedback to achieve their task may face a major challenge in maintaining stability due to the inherently unpredictable nature of their environment. For a robot designed to jump and navigate on soft surfaces, successful trajectory planning is crucial and can be achieved by incorporating feedback into the control system. This paper presents an optimal control strategy that uses feedback to help a robot hop along a predetermined path, even one with an irregular shape, by minimizing the effects of nonlinear dynamics and uncertain factors like gravity and friction. This approach, which combines the capabilities of trajectory planning and optimal control, allows for feedback to be calculated at every point along the path, thus significantly reducing the influence of uncertainties. By applying this method to a robot model, we are able to analyze its ability to follow different reference paths and assess the benefits of using feedback in terms of tracking precision, energy efficiency and stability. Furthermore, we demonstrate that using a careful selection of reference paths can improve the robot's ability to follow these paths by reducing its center of gravity, thus enhancing its overall performance.

This study explores the use of Concurrent Transmissions (CT) to enhance the scalability and reliability of firmware updates in massive IoT systems. To assess the effectiveness of CT, we analyzed its limits in a system where numerous devices receive packets over an LTE-A Pro network. Given the CT's potential drawbacks - a smaller gain than expected and a high failure rate - we propose a practical method to fully realize CT's benefits. This approach identifies recoverable devices and adjusts the transmission strategy to ensure all devices can receive a complete and error-free update. Building on this idea, we developed a protocol, PROD-CT, for optimizing CT-based updates. Compared to the standard approach, PROD-CT yields a notable 66.6% increase in successful updates, along with a 2-fold improvement in network efficiency, when considering the same amount of overhead.

Quantum systems that experience many-body localization (MBL) exhibit a complex thermal phase diagram with intricate, non-ergodic structures when exposed to strong disorder. In this complex phase diagram, the percolation of energy localization across different energy shells spans a temperature range from the MBL threshold down to the thermodynamic limit. A key aspect of this problem is the investigation into how the spatial branching of localization islands and the associated fractal properties behave across this phase transition and how they relate to the scaling of entanglement entropy with respect to system size.

To address this, researchers have developed a theoretical framework that incorporates a detailed statistical analysis of the propagation of energy localization and the associated fractal properties across the MBL phase transition. Using this framework, researchers have shown that the fractal dimension associated with the self-energy of localized states changes smoothly across the MBL phase transition, whereas in ergodic thermal states, it exhibits a linear relationship. In contrast, in non-ergodic, delocalized many-body localized states, it maintains a linear relationship. Moreover, researchers have discovered a critical exponent $\alpha$ that governs how the fractal properties of localization islands and the associated entropy scale with respect to system size, and how the $\alpha$ parameter changes across the MBL phase transition.

To further investigate the relationships, researchers have employed a novel labeling approach to the lattice in both configuration and permutation spaces across the MBL phase transition. In configuration space, it was found that the occupation of sites

The pattern extraction algorithm known as Breakable Matrix Discovery has several efficient variants that quickly identify target patterns within given data sets.  A new variant of this algorithm, known as kBM-DP+, has been developed to address the complex MultipleTargets problem.  By simplifying the pattern extraction problem and utilizing previously established results, the algorithm was designed to improve computational efficiency.  When compared to existing approaches, the algorithm requires significantly reduced runtime and memory usage.  A new theoretical bound has also been established for the number of extracted patterns, resulting in a proven upper limit for the algorithm's memory requirements.  Furthermore, the algorithm's ability to accurately extract patterns was demonstrated through a comprehensive analysis of its target patterns and runtime complexity.  Based on these findings, the algorithm's practicality and effectiveness for extracting relevant patterns within given data sets can be assessed.  Ultimately, the algorithm's ability to quickly and accurately extract patterns was showcased through several challenging datasets, showcasing its potential as a powerful pattern extraction tool.

Our investigation delves into the presence of adversarial examples in quantum classifiers. Since current evaluation metrics, primarily designed for binary classification, are inadequate for assessing their robustness, we develop a weighted average precision metric. We then examine the performance of two popular quantum classifiers on both robust and non-robust adversarial strategies against different types of adversarial attacks. Additionally, to gauge the sensitivity of these models, we employ three specific attacks against which we compare their performance. Our analysis reveals that these models exhibit a mix of robust and non-robust outcomes on distinct datasets and attack scenarios. Given the diversity of outcomes across these scenarios, we suggest customizing evaluation metrics and classification assessment strategies according to the specific adversarial scenario in consideration.

We analyze the asymptotic behavior of spectral parameters in a spherical 
domain given by the unit sphere with a specific boundary condition specified by 
the heat kernel. We examine eigenvalues for two cases: those governed by the 
Steklov problem and the Neumann problem. Recent findings by Gaudrey and Ginzburg 
indicated a specific behavior among spectral parameters in a spherical domain 
for a particular type of boundary condition and eigenvalues. Our study 
demonstrates that in a spherical domain for a specified class of integers, 
certain volume-normalized eigenvalues exhibit a consistent pattern. We use 
the heat kernel to examine the Neumann problem and show a consistent pattern 
among spectral parameters. Our study combines recent findings from K. De lathaupt 
and M. Slepcev by using a phase field equation with a particular type of 
homogenization, and recent findings from M. Gharaletou by using the heat kernel 
exactly.

This paper introduces a novel technique for aligning control-flow traces called the spine alignment, specifically designed for real-time and off-line usage. It offers a more general approach to the phase-locking problem, allowing for a common frame of reference across multiple processes, even in the presence of missing events. In contrast to conventional methods, spine alignment focuses on phase synchronization rather than event synchronization, utilizing the events as landmarks along the paths as references for the alignment process. As such, it can accommodate complex paths and event distributions, providing flexibility in the analysis of process executions. Although this flexibility comes at the cost of additional uncertainties in the analysis, the authors conducted a case study on the Linux kernel to demonstrate the benefits of this approach, revealing new insights into the kernel's behavior that could otherwise go unnoticed in traditional alignment analyses.

Advanced wireless communication systems require precise radio propagation modeling to operate effectively. Traditional methods, including ray tracing and physical statistics models, offer accuracy but at a significant computational cost. Recent developments in deep learning have improved predictive capabilities for communication systems. This paper presents an innovative 3D radio propagation prediction method based on a deep convolutional neural network. In contrast to prior approaches, our method achieves high accuracy using simplified measurement datasets and caters to diverse environmental conditions. We describe the development of a large-scale dataset for indoor scenarios and evaluate the proposed model against a physical statistics based alternative. Our results demonstrate that this deep learning technique provides estimated path loss with a standard deviation of approximately 2.4 dB, while the physical statistics model has a standard deviation of 3.0 dB. We observed that the error ranges of these methods show significant correlation. Nevertheless, this deep learning method's estimated lower error bounds are closer to the physical statistics model's average values than would be expected under Gaussian distribution assumptions.

Validation algorithms for temporal planning systems aim to verify if a generated plan aligns with the intentions of the agent. Success in plan validation boosts the overall system performance by minimizing incorrect or incomplete plans obtained from partial representations of the problem. However, even with significant advancements, validity-based approaches still struggle to resolve plan feasibility on complex real-world problems. This paper proposes the 'lifted action sequences' method for accelerating plan validation: a pattern extraction technique that identifies and groups recurring patterns of actions within an online plan. These identified patterns can provide hints to the plan validation algorithm to move on towards the goal by pinpointing the actions that are least likely to contribute to the plan's feasibility. Our 'lifted action sequences' method was thoroughly tested and the results show that the plan validity algorithm can achieve improvements of up to 10.6 times faster than before, while also reducing the time required to detect pattern occurrences by 2.9 times.

No-or-low generation capacity is a critical factor in power system resilience and emergency response planning. This concept is challenging to model, especially when detailed timeframes are not utilized, as costs are increased by poor resource allocation and inefficient time resolution. This study introduces an approach to evaluate the efficiency of time-based modeling by comparing physical constraints with relaxed formulations and finds that the linearization errors converge over time. The complexity of multi-period modeling is compared to the cost of modeling at a coarser time scale, revealing that improving time resolution is justified if a certain level of generation capacity is at risk. The methodology also enables the calculation of a minimum time resolution required to ensure a certain level of efficiency in resource allocation. A numerical example using PSS SINCAL demonstrates the significance of temporal resolution in power system planning.

For the ionic Vlasov-Poisson models, we have investigated various boundary conditions for computational simulations. Specifically, we considered Dirichlet, Neumann, and mixed boundary conditions for the Poisson equation within the context of periodic boundary conditions for the electron and ion phases. Our focus is on the scenario where the computational domain of the electron distribution function does not include a sheath; hence, we specify zero electric potential at the boundary in line with previous studies. Consequently, the associated electric field is continuous at the boundary, leading to the derivation of mixed boundary conditions for the electric potential of the ion phase via the electric field of the electron phase. We have extensively verified these boundary conditions through various numerical experiments to ensure their robustness. Furthermore, we have used these boundary conditions to develop and test a kinetic-Poisson model that models the coupling between the electron and ion phases through the Poisson equation and the Vlasov equation. Our numerical results demonstrate the satisfactory performance of the kinetic-Poisson model in comparison with an Euler-Poisson model that captures the essential features of a plasma fluid motion model.

To optimize the quality of search results, developers can utilize search terms that accurately represent the rest of their search query. This study focuses on finding relevant search terms using the API documentation available in source code comments. Since comments provide concise information about functions, developers can leverage this information to identify suitable search terms. By extracting sentences from comments, the research proposes two graph-based ranking algorithms - TextRank and POSRank - that analyze sentence structures to enhance search term quality. These ranking algorithms were embedded in a novel search method called Graph-Assisted Search (GAS), which demonstrates superior performance in retrieving relevant documents compared to conventional search methods. An evaluation was conducted using 30 Java projects to assess the effectiveness of their proposed method.

This research explores the occurrence of ultrasound-assisted fluidization through the shear-induced instability phenomenon in viscoelastic gels under the influence of ultrasound.  A thin layer of carbopol gel, sandwiched between two plates with varying air pressures, was studied as the model system.  The dynamic fluidization patterns and periodic shifts in the fluidized and non-fluidized regions were recorded for diverse ultrasound intensities, and correlated with the acoustic properties of the gel layer, consisting of echo and transmission signals.  Our findings indicate that the changes in the gel's fluidization behavior and acoustic characteristics are directly proportional to the ultrasound power applied.  Furthermore, the period of the oscillations in the gel's fluidization state is directly dependent on the inverse square root of the applied pressure difference and the square root of the ultrasound frequency used.  This study not only provides evidence of the shear-induced instability mechanism but also offers a non-invasive method for characterizing the shear stress and shear viscosity required to demonstrate the Palierne model for gas-liquid flow through a porous medium.

This note presents a streamlined version of the mathematical induction proof for the Collatz conjecture, utilizing the key insight that certain initial conditions yield a finite set of values to leverage as a 'halting set' to terminate the recursive process. By identifying a specific initial value, we can establish the conjecture's validity for all positive integers and ultimately prove the Collatz conjecture.

This research aims to understand how Explainable AI techniques can enhance our understanding of document classification decision-making processes. By applying XAI methods to a dataset of classified documents, we can uncover key features driving the models' conclusions. Using a dataset of classified documents from the TREC Karpathakoset, we can evaluate the effectiveness of XAI techniques in highlighting relevant details. The ultimate goal is to leverage these methods for continuous model validation, enabling the detection of potential errors or inconsistencies in machine learning models during operation. This could, in turn, facilitate the development of more robust AI systems.

In an open, transparent, and efficient market-based system for stable matches, we investigated how a transparent and visible rating system affects the behavior of a large number of self-interested agents and the performance of the matching outcomes. We demonstrated through theoretical and experimental analysis that when agents publicly rate each other's utility performance in the market, it results in matching outcomes of optimal stability. Notably, our experiments found that while free riding on ratings is a potential issue, it does not impede the market's ability to achieve stable matchings. Additionally, we observed that the free rider problem significantly diminishes when the number of ratings required to assess agent utility is substantial.

The assessment of automatic summarization remains a subject of ongoing research.
The current methods for evaluating summaries compare them to reference summaries in terms of
similarity, but these measures are lacking as they do not account for diversity and there's a
disconnection between the scores given by these methods and human evaluations. To address this
issue, we developed SummScore, a novel evaluation metric that focuses on representing a set of
summaries as a single, diverse mixture. This is achieved by having multiple generated summaries
explore different representation spaces, allowing for a score that closely matches human evaluations
and promotes diverse summaries. In our experiments, SummScore showed a stronger connection to
human evaluations compared to existing methods, and it also included a new metric that focuses on
diversity. Furthermore, SummScore was used to evaluate existing summary evaluation metrics and it
was found that ROUGE-1 was the only one that was able to effectively evaluate a diverse set of
summaries. Finally, SummScore was used to provide new insights when evaluating the state of the
art in various summary evaluation tasks, and it was also shown that by optimizing the diversity of the
summaries generated by a model, it was also possible to optimize the scores given by ROUGE-1, thus
bridging the gap between human evaluations and automatic evaluation metrics.

In sparsity-driven algorithms like Compressed Sensing, practical applications 
often struggle with the significant number of measurements required due to 
processing large datasets.  This research contributes a new perspective to 
address this challenge by investigating how to recover sparsity in one context 
while utilizing sparsity from another.  The goal is to overcome the need for 
very high numbers of measurements, only requiring cross-correlated data from 
the other context.  Our study provides a theoretical framework, revealing how the 
capacity to recover sparsity increases with more cross-correlated data and 
decreases with additional noise.  This concept is then demonstrated across 
three distinct domains: computer vision using wavelet and Fourier sparsity, 
and the recovery of binary strings from related and unrelated datasets.
